WITNESS XXXII (V ex off.)

Sr. ANNA SERAFINA GREGORI

Scope in the process: From Sess. 326th of 19 November 1917 (fol. 2754) to Sess. 329th of 22 November 1917 (fol. 2779v.).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Francesca Gregori, born on 5 June 1856 at Rome.

State and profession: Religious in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, directress of the house of Palermo.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness when she came to know the Servant of God: 36 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness came to know her: 61 years.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 61 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: From her entrance into the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne (1892) until the death of the Servant of God, the witness, who resided in the House of Palermo, maintained continual contacts with the Superior General and frequent meetings.

(We omit the present testimony, because it brings no new elements of proof).

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 2756, testis respondit:

§ 684
General details of the witness.

My name in the world is Francesca Gregori, I was born in Rome on 5 June 1856, daughter of the late Count Girolamo and Baroness Luisa Carpegna.

In April 1892 I entered this Institute, and made my profession the following year for St. Anne.

My first offices were to establish in the Church attached to this House the Congregation of the Daughters of Mary, and to teach Catechism to the children. And two years after I had been here, I was sent to Palermo to open a school, which has since gone on developing, and now comprises the elementary schools for boys and for girls, the complementary ones and those of further training for girls.

This is one of the principal Institutes of Palermo, and I have been its Directress for 23 years.

WITNESS XXXIII
Most Rev. Fr. GIOACCHINO CORRADO

Scope in the process: Sess. 331st of 10 January 1918 (fol. 2792).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Gioacchino Corrado, born on 9 March 1835 at Rome.

State and profession: Priest, Rector General of the Congregation of the Clerics Regular of the Mother of God, consultor of Propaganda Fide and of the Apostolic Dataria.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 83 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: The witness does not reveal the date when his dealings with the Servant of God began, with whom, however, he was in relation for about six years.

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: The present testimony is useful for knowing the esteem Gattorno enjoyed in ecclesiastical circles.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 2795v., testis respondit:

§ 685
General details of the witness.

My name is Gioacchino Corrado, son of the late Pietro and Giovanna Cori. I was born in Rome on 9 March 1835. I entered the Congregation of the Clerics Regular of the Mother of God in 1852; I was ordained a Priest; I have held various offices in my Congregation, of which I am at present Rector General. I have been Consultor of five Sacred Congregations, and now I am still Consultor of Propaganda Fide and of the Apostolic Dataria.

Ad 6: I come to depose because I have been legitimately summoned. What I shall say is from my own knowledge, because I knew the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno personally and heard her confession for six years, in the time when she was in Rome, when she made the first foundation in Rome at Vicolo Margana.

Ad 8: I have great admiration for the Servant of God, and from the time I came to know her, I foresaw how it would end, and how one day the Process of Beatification would be begun.

§ 686
Family life and foundation of the Institute.

Ad 9: I know that the Servant of God was born in Genoa of a rich banker; that she was a wife for some years. I know of a daughter of hers, whom she herself afterward placed in marriage. I know that she would not hear of a second marriage, although left a widow quite young; and of her childhood, youth and life in the world I know nothing else.

Of her foundation, then, and of her religious life, I can say that she was always a most exemplary and most active Religious, so that at her death she left her Institute most flourishing in Italy, and spread also outside Europe.

Of the Constitutions of her Institute I know that in the Congregation they were much questioned, but that Mgr. Schiaffino, then Secretary of the Sacred Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, knew how to defend them so well that they were approved on an experimental basis. I found that the Sisters were informed by an excellent spirit, and in their simplicity most exemplary.

I know that the cares she had, as a diligent and prudent mother, for her daughter Carlotta, did not in any way distract her from zeal, love, activity for her Institute.

§ 687
A woman of great faith and deep piety.

I understood, from the way she made her confession, that she was a woman of great faith and deep piety, and that she had a special devotion to Jesus in the Sacrament and that she fostered this devotion much among her Sisters. She was completely detached from this world, not knowing what to do with her riches. She worked very hard for the schools and for the Christian education of girls, and for the care of the sick women.

The Servant of God was of great prudence, as I could see from her government, and from the criteria by which she governed. She was a prudent and resolute spiritual mother.

I always held her to be a holy woman, but I could not say anything else, either of her life or of her death.

I have heard other persons speak too, and they attest their esteem and veneration for the Servant of God, as of a holy woman, and I have never heard anything said against her.

WITNESS XXXV (III cont. ex off.)

Most Rev. Mgr. CAMILLO MANGOT

Scope in the process: Sess. 333rd of 1 May 1918 (fol. 2806v.).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Camillo Mangot, born on 17 March 1850 at Bettola (Piacenza).

State and profession: Priest, canon provost of the Cathedral of Piacenza.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 68 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: The witness knew the Servant of God in his capacity as Secretary of His Excellency Mgr. Scalabrini, Bishop of Piacenza.

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: The present testimony allows us to know the thought and the relations Mgr. Scalabrini had with the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 2810, testis respondit:

§ 689
General details of the witness.

My name is Camillo Mangot; I was born at Bettola, Diocese and Province of Piacenza, on 17 March 1850, son of the late Giovanni and Giulia Ghizzoni. I was educated first in the Seminary of Borgo S. Donnino, then in the Alberoni College, and was ordained a Priest in 1873. I was

p. 451

XXXV witness (III cont. ex off.), Most Rev. Mgr. C. Mangot 451 for about 30 years Secretary to Mgr. Scalabrini, Bishop of Piacenza, and then Canon Provost of the Cathedral, a dignity which I still hold; and now I am temporarily at Rieti, requested by that Bishop to make up for the great shortage of Clergy in this time of war.

§ 690
Scope of knowledge.

Ad 7: I knew the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno personally, but never had particular dealings with her. I have, however, often heard her spoken of by Mgr. Scalabrini and by some Parish Priest, and also by her Sisters.

Mgr. Scalabrini spoke to me of her as a very intelligent woman and quite virtuous; he noted, however, that the discipline of the Mother House was a little too easygoing, that is, he noted that outsiders were received a little too often in the reception room; I believe, however, that these persons went only to deal with matters relating to the Institute. When in some rare circumstance she gave a lunch, for example to the Cardinal Protector, who had arrived there, it was, in the Bishop's judgment, of somewhat excessive generosity, and the Bishop himself also did not like that the Sisters themselves should serve at table, although at lunch there were only ecclesiastics and some relative of the Servant of God. The courses that were then served at table were at least three.

As to discipline, the said Bishop further noted that there was too much ease of access because of an internal door of communication with the family of the Servant of God.

It also made an impression on him that at the end of the said lunches the daughter of the Servant of God would appear with her little girl to pay respects to the Cardinal and stay on in conversation.

§ 691
Mgr. Scalabrini and the Servant of God.

A Cardinal Protector having died, I think Cardinal Verga, before the successor was appointed, in the meantime Mgr. Scalabrini was charged by the Holy Father with the Protectorate of the Institute, and he made use of it to give the order that the door of communication between the house of the Religious and that of the Servant of God's son-in-law be closed, a communication that was inside the House. I know that already earlier Mgr. Scalabrini had pointed out this inconvenience to the Servant of God, which did not make a good impression on some. When Mgr. Scalabrini ordered the closing of the said door, the Servant of God wrote him a letter, which I still keep (and which, as soon as I return to Piacenza, I shall search for to transmit to this tribunal) in which she set out the reasons why that door had until then been open. I possess other letters of the Servant of God to Mgr. Scalabrini, which I shall likewise hand over to this tribunal, but they are of no importance. I recall that in several the Servant of God invited him to clothing ceremonies; and the Bishop marveled at the fruitfulness, which he called prodigious, of her Institute. He thought there was too much ease on the part of the Servant of God in the acceptance of Postulants at the beginning of her Institute. Yet he excused her, because it was the beginning; he never told me, however, that she took unworthy ones. I wish to declare that he did not hold the acceptance of postulants against her.

I know well that Mgr. Scalabrini modified his judgments about the Servant of God in the course of time, in this sense: that his esteem of the virtues of the Servant of God grew.

I possess all the writings of Mgr. Scalabrini: I have not, however, had leisure to examine them all. When I return to Piacenza, I shall go through them as completely as I can and, finding anything there about the Servant of God, I shall submit it to this Sacred Tribunal.

Most devout as Mgr. Scalabrini was to the Most Blessed Sacrament, he sought to spread devotion to it as far as he could throughout the Diocese, and exhorted the Servant of God to accept the Institute of the Deaf-mutes, which he entrusted to her, in order to choose among these girls elements to make them Perpetual Adorers of the Most Blessed Sacrament; and the Servant of God put this idea into practice with great enthusiasm. In memory of the first clothing ceremony, then, which took place of these deaf-mute Adorers, I had executed, at the commission of Mgr. Scalabrini, a painting representing the Servant of God in the act of clothing four of these Adorers. This picture is now kept by the Missionaries of St. Charles.

§ 692
Reputation for holiness.

I for my part always held the Servant of God as a Holy woman: her serenity and imperturbable calm even in the midst of her tribulations and troubles impressed me. Her penances were also reported to me, especially as to night rest and food. It was also noticed that, while for others she was generous and very fond of the decorum of the house, she herself made do with little in food and sleep.

I have also heard her spoken of by many in general, both of the people and

p. 453

XXXVI witness (VI ex off.), Sr. Anna Angela Pedrazzini 453 of the Clergy, as a Holy woman. I have never heard anyone speak ill of her. Perhaps it was Mgr. Scalabrini himself who told me that Fr. Tornatore saw the Servant of God in a dream before making her personal acquaintance. I must note that Fr. Tornatore, a Lazarist, was in Piacenza held to be a saint by everyone.

I must also say that Mgr. Scalabrini was somewhat strict concerning the table of the Clergy during Pastoral Visits, and did not allow more than two courses. Otherwise he would turn the plate over and say enough.

WITNESS XXXVIII (VIII ex off.)

Sr. ANNA AMANTE LA BARBERA

Scope in the process: From Sess. 337th of 7 April 1919 (fol. 2840) to Sess. 342nd of 14 April 1919 (fol. 2885); also from Sess. 346th of 2 March 1921 (fol. 2918) to Sess. 356th of 16 April 1921 (fol. 2991v.).

XXXVIII witness (VIII ex off.), Sr. A. Amante La Barbera 455

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Carmela La Barbera, born on 25 September 1860 at Palermo.

State and profession: Religious in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, formerly local Superior.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness when she came to know the Servant of God: 22 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness came to know her: 51 years.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 59-61 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: From her entrance into religious life (20 July 1882) to the death of the Mother Foundress, the witness had repeated occasions to know her very well.

For reasons of brevity, the answers from no. 3 to 21 are omitted, because they are irrelevant information.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 2844, testis respondit:

§ 695
General details of the witness.

My name in the world is Carmela La Barbera. I was born on 25 September 1860, daughter of the late Andrea and Giuseppina Basile, in Palermo. I was brought up as a Christian, especially by my mother. My father, who was a Garibaldian, was not yet confirmed when I entered religious life. He opposed me strongly beforehand to prevent me from entering religious life, but before dying he asked my forgiveness.

I entered the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne on 20 July 1882 in the House of Piacenza, and was received by the Foundress herself, Mother Rosa Gattorno, and the name Sr. Anna Amante was given me; and it was Sr. Anna del Salvatore Orsi (who had changed my mind and led me to become a nun) who suggested this name for me to Mother Gattorno. I took the Religious habit on 25 July of the same year. At the beginning of the following September I was sent to Orbetello; after a few months from there I was sent to Siena. I made my first vows the following year (1883) for the feast of St. Anne.

§ 696
Foundation of the Institute and style of government.

Ad 22, Proc. fol. 2858: She was the first Superior of the Institute, although she did not feel up to commanding others, as she told me.

The Servant of God never wanted to be called Mother General, and woe if she saw it in the addresses of the letters sent to her: she wanted to be called simply Mother. She told me that Pio Nono had commanded her to direct the Institute. This office, in all the time she held it, which was until the end of her life, she discharged as a true Mother and with great intelligence.

In the acceptance of Postulants (and I brought her many) she said to me: «Pray, make the novena to the Holy Spirit, and have the Postulants make it too, and test them». She herself prayed, as she assured me, and said to me: «Do not send her to me until I write it to you». And only when she felt sure, then she wrote me to bring them to her.

As to the dowry she was not demanding, and said to me: «If they have no dowry, it does not matter, they will make it themselves».

I have heard from some Sister of the oldest that the Servant of God was accused, I do not know by whom, of being easy in the admission of Postulants at the beginning of the Institute; but I do not know the grounds of this appraisal. As far as I know, she was always most prudent. And the same Sisters who spoke to me of it deplored such an accusation.

§ 697
Visits to the communities.

She often visited all her Houses, and with great diligence. She did not omit to visit her Houses even in the last year of her life, and her last journey was to visit the houses of Genoa, Sampierdarena, etc.

In the visits she proceeded in this way. First of all she entered the Church or Chapel to pray for some twenty minutes, as I myself saw in my houses of Prato and Florence. As she came out, the Sisters, all lined up, made a fuss of her, and for all she had a gesture, an affectionate word. She then withdrew to her room for a while, alone. In this connection I recall that on the first visit she made to the House of Florence, when I was there, I had tried to prepare her room as suitably as I was able (at Prato I was too poor to do this). When the Servant of God had withdrawn, she took everything she judged superfluous, made a bundle of it, and, appearing at the door, called me with this bundle in her hand, and having me beside her, said to me: «Listen, Amante, these things are not for me. Do you not think of our vow of poverty? Bring me an old blanket», and added so many things to me about poverty that she made me weep, and I promised her not to repeat this mistake.

Ad 23, Proc. fol. 2872: The Institute spread very rapid-

p. 457

XXXVIII witness (VIII ex off.), Sr. A. Amante La Barbera 457 ly, and in the Mother's lifetime one could already count more than three hundred houses, in Italy, in Spain, in America, in Africa.

§ 698
She made use of relatives for some affairs of the Institute.

Ad 24: After founding the Institute, the Servant of God made use of her brothers for various affairs of the same Institute. I recall that Federico obtained for her the reduction, from which we benefit, on railway tickets, and that he helped her in the building of this Generalate House. I saw that her daughter Carlotta often came to visit her, but I also saw that many times the Mother sent her away, especially when Sisters from outside came, with whom naturally the Mother had to confer.

She had much to suffer from her son-in-law, Count Gaspare Barbiellini. Because of him I saw her weep, and heard her exclaim: «My God! Relatives are our ruin. But what is to be done, O Lord, if You have given them to me». And alluding to the son-in-law she said, I do not know if only once: «In hell there are better ones than he!». On this subject I have a great confusion in my head, and I would not be able to recount any particular fact. I recall, however, that it was always a matter of money interests, and the son-in-law continually wanted money. I myself heard the Servant of God say to the Secretaries: «If they come today (that is, those of her daughter's family) say that I cannot receive them».

The Barbiellini lived in the House adjoining this one on the South side, and I ascertained that they always had to come by the street side, with the order that the bell be rung in a certain way, as a sign that they were entering, and this annoyed Barbiellini, who sometimes would not have wished it. «We are relatives, we, and there is no need to notify the Mother». Once I myself heard him say to his children, pointing to the premises of this House: «See, all this is ours». Once, as he was passing through Florence with his daughter, who was engaged, and the fiancé, while I was serving them a small refreshment, I heard him say to the future son-in-law: «This too is ours». It was precisely when I reported this to the Servant of God that she exclaimed: «In hell there are better ones than he».

With these relatives I had no contact, because truly they were not among my sympathies. In her last illness the Servant of God determined who among the Sisters was to attend her in turns. She included Fr. Vincenzo, Capuchin and our Chaplain, Fr. Agostino, a Minim, and added: «Do not let anyone else enter». Once, however, her daughter Carlotta entered; she blessed her and with a gesture invited her to go out. How I felt when, the Servant of God being dead, the granddaughter Maria opened with her father a cupboard near the grandmother's room, believing she would find something of value there, being then disappointed, and entered the room apostrophizing the corpse with these words: «As grandmother I respect you, as General I make war on you», anyone can imagine! And about the relatives I could not say anything else.

§ 699
Serenity of the Servant of God during the Apostolic Visitation.

Ad 25: When the Apostolic Visitation came, the Servant of God trusted everything to her Crucifix, and to me, who was all agitated, she said: «The Visitor will go to various Houses: the Lord and the Holy Mother will make the truth known to him, but he will not reach you». And so it was, since he never came to Tuscany. The Mother too was a little afflicted, and said to me: «It is the devil who wants me agitated: but I must trust in my Crucifix». And I never heard from her a complaint for this. And although she told me that the Visitor would not reach me, she added: «If, however, he should come, you will tell him everything, and you will open your soul to him». And this exhortation I heard repeated to the other Superiors. Of that Apostolic Visitation I know nothing else.

Ad 26, Proc. fol. 2878v.: I saw the Servant of God always observe the precepts of God, of the Church and the obligations of her state, even in the minutiae.

§ 700
Life of faith and prayer.

Ad 27: The Servant of God possessed and exercised the Theological and Cardinal virtues, poverty, humility and the other connected ones. And as to Faith, I myself heard her say: «Would that I could go and give my blood and my life for the faith».

She exhorted us to apply ourselves to catechetical instruction of children; and here in the Church attached to the Generalate House such instruction was given.

I once told the Mother that I intended to give a little mission to men in our Chapel. The Servant of God was greatly consoled, encouraged me and told me to come to an agreement with the Cardinal (then Bausa). I then carried out my project for several years with consoling results, which greatly gladdened our Mother. The Mother wanted and imposed on us to act as Missionaries in the Hospi-

p. 459

XXXVIII witness (VIII ex off.), Sr. A. Amante La Barbera 459 tals, first by our bearing, then by charity and finally by the word.

How she prayed, the Servant of God! She attended to her office, yes, but she took advantage of any little time to go before the Sacrament; and the manner? One had to see her: she seemed a statue! Always kneeling on the ground, kneeling and leaning with her hands on a chair, she seemed to feel nothing any more of what was happening around her! One could call her, and even shake her, she did not answer. In all other prayers too, outside the Chapel or Church, she was seen supremely recollected, and in particular I recall the blessing of the table, at which she was present, but never wished to give, with hands joined, how recollected she was seen to be! Even outside prayer her soul appeared always united with God, so that those who had the good fortune to speak with her, if outsiders, said afterward: «Your Mother is a Saint».

Also in the recreations her union with God was noticed. She took, yes, an active part in the conversation: she burst into joyful laughter, but suddenly she was seen all recollected, and we were intent on observing her. To us she used to say: «Recreate yourselves, yes, but always in the presence of God». «Meditation», she said, «is my first pasture»; and she often made it (when she was suffering) before her Crucifix, as she told me; and never neglected it.

§ 701
Devotions of the Servant of God.

Proc. fol. 2888: She had such devotion to the Most Holy Trinity, which she always mentioned.

In everything she commended herself to the Eternal Father, and gave us an oil which she said the Eternal Father blessed; and this oil has worked many graces.

For the Divine Son, then, she lived, she always worked for him.

In the life of Our Lord, however, what formed her delights was the Mystery of the Crucifixion. From herself and from a sister of hers I know that from childhood the Crucifix was what drew her heart.

§ 702
Hope and trust in the Lord.

Proc. fol. 2936v.: The Servant of God lived on hope: her Crucifix was her life, was her all. In the world and in men she never placed her heart. She hoped to attain Paradise, toward which her aspirations were directed, through the mercy of God, because she said that she was the most unworthy of all. When our savings were brought to her (this I say not only for my own case, but also because I was present at various conversations of hers with other Superiors), the first thing she asked us was this: «But first of all tell me, how do you treat the Sisters? Do you let them lack anything, do you make them suffer? Mind well, you hear, because otherwise this money would burn me».

§ 703
Prudence and justice.

Proc. fol. 2947: Prudence: All her actions she directed to God, as appeared from her talk and from her works. The principal means she employed to obtain the eternal salvation of others were prayers and works of charity.

She was never heard, as far as I know, to take part in or to make talk either frivolous or of little usefulness. I know, in general, that she took counsel before deciding anything important, either with Bishops or with other wise persons, and, as I said in another session, she prayed. She never showed liking or dislike for any of her daughters. I know from my own personal experience that the Mother used great tact with her daughters: sometimes she yielded to their reluctances so as not to dishearten and disconcert them, and by all she was esteemed as very prudent. In spending she was neither prodigal nor tight. Woe to us if we had made an expense on luxury things, and I myself received from her a strong rebuke in such cases.

Confiding in the Servant of God, we were perfectly tranquil, because we knew that whatever we had deposited in her heart never came out again, without our needing to recommend to her to keep it to herself.

Justice: If anyone wished to leave something to the Institute, she inquired before accepting whether there were among his relatives any needy persons or persons who had a right to it, and only in the negative case decided to accept.

§ 704
Spirit of mortification.

Proc. fol. 2953: In temperance too her virtue shone. I have heard from the usual Sisters who lived closer to the Mother that, from childhood, the Servant of God so loved the poor that for them she deprived herself of food to distribute it to them. Having become a widow, she began her life of continual abstinences. She no longer took either meat or broth. And yet meat and especially salami pleased her very much,

p. 461

XXXVIII witness (VIII ex off.), Sr. A. Amante La Barbera 461 as she expressed herself confidentially to me. And to mortify herself the more, she often went to the kitchen on feast days to cut us the portions of salami; she no longer tasted anything sweet, nor fruit. I even saw her many times remain almost fasting with only the soup, because the dishes were prepared with too much care. To our insistence she answered: «No, no, daughters», and delicately pushed the dishes away. I do not know how that body could sustain itself with so little food. She never ate outside meals, I never saw her take anything of food or drink, except on some rare occasions to quench the burning thirst in the great heat of summer; and to resist she rather resorted to plunging her hands into cold water, and so she continued her torment of thirst.

She warmly recommended temperance to us, and also said to us: «When you eat a plate of beans, beware of greed».

§ 705
Sentiments of deep and sincere humility.

Proc. fol. 2961: Most humble was our Mother; she declared herself the greatest sinner, the worst of all, capable of nothing, and that her Crucifix was what carried the House and the Institute forward. And when she said these expressions, one saw her inner persuasion, and that she deeply felt their truth, according to her. If a Sister put «Mother General» on the address of letters, she sent the address back. Once she did it with me too, writing to me at the same time: «Do not venture ever again to call me Mother General». She was fearful of having to render account to God for her Institute. «It would be good», she said, «if they put another in my place for the good of the Institute, but when I am obliged to it, I cannot abandon it». «Without humility, without charity, without observance of the holy rules», she said to us, «one does not enter Paradise». As she taught us, in the care of the sick she lent herself to the most menial services.

When one conversed with her, she enjoyed our thoughts, although in talent and in culture she could have kept us all in our place. She knew French, could play the piano, sang with a beautiful voice, embroidered finely, and yet she told us that she did not know how to say anything, that she did not know how to do anything. She never spoke of herself.

As to perseverance until death in the exercise of all the virtues narrated above, I can declare that the Servant of God exercised them constantly and never relaxed her fervor even for a moment; and I declare that I renew the oath on this particular point.

§ 706
She exercised the virtues to a heroic degree.

Ad 28: The Servant of God exercised all and each of the virtues described above, without exception, to a heroic degree, that is, as if she lived a life above the senses, wholly absorbed in the life of Jesus Christ, and therefore with ease, with facility, with constancy, as if they were connatural to her, in short as so many Saints whose lives I have read exercised them: and from this assertion I exclude no virtue. I could not say which excelled in her, except the charity of God which gathers them all.

Ad 29: The Servant of God, in the exercise of the said virtues, I do not know that she ever exceeded in any way, nor that, because of the mortifications of her body, she rendered herself less fit for the direction of her Institute. To the end she answered her more distant daughters, such as those of America: so that her letters were ordinarily 20 or 25 a day, and we keep a letter addressed by her to a Sister, which had to be broken off because of the aggravation of her last illness.

§ 707
Held in the repute of a saint.

Ad 38, Proc. fol. 2984v.: During the life of the Servant of God, the opinion and the fame of her virtues was that of a Saint. Finding myself more than once at the Florence station to receive the Servant of God, it happened that I saw the Station Master, and even porters, stop to look at our Mother, and then, asked who she was, add: «But that is an extraordinary woman!». We also had great trust in the efficacy of her prayers: and this was general both among the Sisters and among all who knew her. After her death the opinion and fame of holiness, and the trust in her help, not only have not ceased, but have increased. I have also heard it said that in many of our Houses in America such opinion, fame and trust are altogether extraordinary. And I know of no artifice employed by anyone and in any place to promote the said opinion, fame or trust. And I cannot attribute the cause to anything other than the luminous examples of virtue offered us in her life and the manifold graces the Lord has granted through her intercession here and there.

§ 708
There were persons opposed to her.

Ad 39: In my presence no one ever dared even to criticize our Mother in anything. But I know that a certain Sr. Eletta (who afterward ended by leaving the Institute, and died shortly after)

p. 463

XXXVIII witness (VIII ex off.), Sr. A. Amante La Barbera 463 made our Mother suffer greatly, writing much against her to the Superiors. Of this one I do not remember the surname: and I know in general that some other was not favorable to the Servant of God, but I could not say any particular; the more so as the Servant of God never spoke to me of it. Of laypeople who did not esteem her, after having known her, I could name no one apart from her son-in-law Barbiellini, but not because he did not see her great virtues, but because self-interest blinded him. After the death of the Servant of God I believe that the greater part of the Sisters who were not favorable to her changed their minds, since I heard some exclaim: «My God, we complained of our first Mother Rosa, who was a Saint!». And now I recall having heard these words from a certain Sr. A. Marta Scalea, and from Sr. A. Tancreda (I do not now remember the surname), both of my house of Florence. But of these two I can say that their opposition did not come from lack of esteem, but from some resentment, natural to our wretchedness, at the corrections received from the Servant of God. Both are now dead.

§ 709
Reputation for holiness and graces after death.

Ad 40: I have heard many Sisters speak of graces obtained through the intercession of the Servant of God after her death, but I am not in a position to report them in particular.

After the death of the Servant of God I was seized by a grave ailment in the left side of the chest, which made me spasm greatly, and for which Professors Grocco and Franchini of Florence and Montechiari of Rome had judged an operation necessary. It was the year 1900. On the night of All Saints I dreamed of the Mother, whom I had invoked so many times in my prayers, and she asked me what I had that I was so afflicted, and I answered her that I had that ailment for which they judged an operation necessary, which I did not want, she felt me with her right hand on the diseased part, saying to me: «But you have nothing, you know»; and she gave me a little slap, as she used to when she was alive. At that little slap I woke up, felt myself at once, and no longer found the swelling or the hardness that had been in the diseased part: I was fully cured. I sent to our Secretary General a certificate of Professor Franchini, which at the next session I shall hand over to this tribunal. I must note that nothing had been decided about my operation, because I did not want to hear of it.

§ 711
General details of the witness and scope of her knowledge.

I was born at Lizzano Belvedere, province of Bologna, on 10 September 1851, daughter of the late Ignazio and Domenica Comparti. My parents were pious and true Christians, and educated their offspring very well. I had presented myself to Cardinal Vannicelli to enter another Institute, but in those very days the Servant of God happened to come to Ferrara, who, when she saw me (presented to her by Mgr. Wanstienkist, the Cardinal's Secretary and my Confessor), said: «This is our first Postulant of this House». On seeing Mother Gattorno I was very well impressed, and although destined for another Institute, I at once very willingly assented to the words of the Servant of God, and, accepted, I was taken by her to Piacenza. On the day of the Immaculate Conception I put on the religious habit, and was sent to the House of Genoa. After four years I made my simple vows, then spent a few months as Sacristan at Piacenza, then was sent to Foligno as cook, where I likewise remained a few months. Then I came to Rome, where I stayed about ten years, and afterward to Pistoia for two or three years as Superior; then I was sent to found the house of Pisa, or rather I opened it during my stay at Pistoia. I was then sent to open the house of Pignatelli in Palermo, where I stayed about two or three years; then finally I was sent to Siena as Superior, an office from which I ceased last year by reason of the present canonical provisions, and there I still am.

I have devotion to our Foundress, and often commend myself to her, because I believe she is powerful at the throne of the Lord, and because I saw her in life work marvelous things.

§ 712
Serenity in danger at Foligno.

The house of Foligno had been opened shortly before by the Servant of God; two days afterward I was there too, as I have said. The Servant of God, who in my opinion foresaw everything, gave us most fervent talks to inflame us in the love of God, and exhorted us to pray much, because in that city they bore us great ill will and would try to harm us. We, on the other hand, heard it said that the libertines bore our Mother great ill will for her art of attracting young women to her Institute, and in fact right in the first times two young women of respectable families, and attractive, had been admitted into our Institute. One evening in particular she recommended us to pray, then we withdrew for rest, but she did not rest. I, who had my room adjoining hers, in communication by a little door, heard that she was praying, and had not gone to bed. I heard her walk for some moments and go near the window, like a person who already knew what was going to happen, and I heard this because of the arrangement of her room, the little door being near the window: when suddenly, toward midnight, the Mother, coming out of her room, called us all in haste, crying: «Come after me, as you are, because they are burning down the house». I put on, as I went, a habit, and the others all in their nightdresses behind her, we went down the stairs through a smoke that took our breath away. The Mother told the Sisters to throw water from the nearby well onto the great door, which was in flames, being sprinkled with petroleum, which gave off a foul stench. The Servant of God with great ease drew back a bolt all rusty (who knows since when it had not been opened) although the flames penetrated inside and the great door, at least in the lower part, was entirely engulfed, because the petroleum had been spilled there so abundantly that our Mother's shoes were all wet from it. The great door being opened by the Servant of God, one saw how the evildoers had propped up bundles of brushwood there, likewise soaked with petroleum. The Servant of God was the first to leap over those flames, and encouraged us others to follow her: I was the second to cross those flames, and then the others also came after, except two who were near the well. The Servant of God meanwhile made use of a wide basin of slaked lime, such as masons use when they slake lime, which was to serve to plaster the future Chapel: she took handfuls of it and threw them on the flames. And so, between the water that the two who remained inside brought and this work of the Mother, the fire was put out. I then saw, with great disgust, the faces of persons who were peeping from behind the windowpanes of the houses opposite, and did not move to help us. All being over, we returned upstairs to the house and the Servant of God had our Sisters, all young and much shaken by fear, given plenty to drink. She did not drink, nor did I. None of us went back to rest. She gave us a fine talk, encouraging us not to fear the devil, who had it in for us, and exhorting us to perfect observance of the Rules.

§ 713
She persevered until death in the exercise of the virtues.

Ad 71, Proc. fol. 3030v.: Of all the Virtues, Theological, Cardinal and connected, of which I have already spoken, I have the firm conviction that the Servant of God persevered in the exercise of them until death, but that she always progressed in them. This was the impression I received when she came to visit my house: I perceived in her an increase each time. And it is still my conviction that the Servant of God practiced the said virtues to a heroic degree: above all charity and humility; that is, that she practiced them with constancy, never drawing back before difficulties and the repugnance which at times one saw she had to overcome; with ease; in short, in a word, as I have read in the lives of many Saints.

The Servant of God enjoyed a reputation for holiness during her life.

§ 714
Reputation for holiness during life.

And this reputation was founded precisely on the virtues that shone in her, on the extraordinary gifts conferred on her by the Lord, of which I have told only a part, but of which I have heard many Sisters speak. And I also know that, even outside the Institute, she enjoyed with various persons, for the same reasons, an esteem of holiness.

And now it comes to my mind that the Servant of God herself, once, telling me that we must hide as much as possible even the supernatural gifts that the Lord may have bestowed, told me that to some person outside the Institute she had disclosed something of her interior, as the Lord had made it known to her, but that of this too she had had to repent, because she received sorrows in return.

I have nothing in particular to say about the death of the Servant of God. Such was my grief at the news of her death that I could not set out on the journey.

§ 715
The reputation for holiness increased after death.

The reputation and opinion of holiness of the Servant of God, both among the Sisters and among outsiders, did not diminish with her death, but grew, and this not by any artifice, but by her virtues and by the graces with which, as both Sisters and some outsider told me, she was made illustrious after her death.

Among the others who esteemed her so highly, I shall also recall the Archbishop of Siena, Mgr. Pierallini, who spoke of her with great reverence, as of a Saint; likewise Mgr. Alberti, his Vicar General. Likewise Mgr. Capponi, Archbishop of Pisa, spoke of her as of a great soul.

§ 718
General details of the witness.

My name is Carlo Santucci, son of the late Luigi and of Maria Calcagni, born at Rome on 9 February 1849, and domiciled at Rome in Piazza della Pigna 6. I am a Lawyer and Senator of the Kingdom. § 719
Claims of the Counts Barbiellini.

The question consisted in this: the Countess Barbiellini and her husband claimed the entire property, and therefore the price obtained from the sale of a house or villa at Sampierdarena, on which Mother Gattorno had placed a mortgage in favor of the spouses Barbiellini, on the occasion of their marriage, as security for a dotal capital of L. 50,000. The spouses Barbiellini, relying on a complex of facts and documents, maintained that the ownership of the house or villa belonged wholly to the Countess, although the cadastral registration was still in the name of the mother, and there existed no formal deed of transfer. And I then gave the opinion that in the strict sense of civil law the thesis of the spouses Barbiellini would be difficult, but that it could be pressed before an ecclesiastical tribunal on the grounds of equity and good faith, given all the circumstances and the arguments alleged. After giving this written opinion, I do not recall having had to concern myself further with the question, and I presume that it was afterward in some way either decided or settled in favor of the spouses Barbiellini, precisely because later I heard no more of it, not even on the occasion of the great judicial case that took place after the death of Mother Gattorno. In this Case I did not wish to take part, because it concerned the alleged nullity of the acts of purchase of certain properties in the name of some fellow Sisters of St. Anne and the nullity of Mother Gattorno's will in favor of the same or of other Daughters of St. Anne.

Count Barbiellini spoke to me of it; but chiefly for moral reasons, given the delicacy of the question, as I have said, I took no part in the Civil Case, and I do not believe either that it took place, even in part, in the Ecclesiastical Tribunals. After a judgment of the Court of Bologna, Barbiellini urged me strongly to attempt a reconciliation of the aforesaid principal dispute, and also of a claim of his, in some way secondary, for the administration he had carried out for many years of his mother-in-law's interests. I attempted a reconciliation with the Most Rev. Mother Carrega, but nothing was achieved, and then the Case went on, I believe with an unfavorable outcome for the Barbiellini.

When Count Barbiellini invited me to intervene for the settlement, he confided to me that his aspirations and his wife's, on the moral side, were limited to that family capital of about three hundred thousand lire, which he believed to be included in the sizable estate of Mother Gattorno, for the most part coming from the liberality of pious persons in favor of the Congregation.

Considering himself defrauded of the family capital, he therefore thought the legal action brought morally justified. He added that he thought he had all the more reason to act, in the interest of the family, because for so many years he had devoted his work to the administration of Mother Gattorno without any recompense. I do not recall that he gave me a convincing demonstration of either claim.

§ 721
General details of the witness.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 82v., testis respondit:

My name is Sr. Anna Maristella Calderone, in the world Rosina, daughter of the late Salvatore and Rosaria Ferra, born in Palermo, aged 52, I am a Religious of the Pious Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, Superior in our House of St. Anne at Ottocalli, Naples, where I live the common life.

Ad 7: I first met the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno in Rome, when I went there as a postulant, that is, in 1884. The following year I was sent to our House at Piacenza, where the Servant of God lived, and I remained in that House from March to October of that year. After leaving Piacenza I saw the Servant of God still many times, but always on some occasion and for community business. She showed herself with me, as with all the Sisters, not as Superior but as a true mother. Then in our community I always heard her spoken of with praise by all the fellow Sisters older than I in vocation, who always recalled with admiration the virtues of the Servant of God. I shall therefore say in this examination what I know personally and what I have been able to hear from others.

Ad 17, Proc. fol. 88: The Servant of God, after founding the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne at Piacenza, put at its head as Superior Sr. A. Francesca Camisa, now deceased and of whom I have always heard spoken with praise. I note that the Servant of God did not take the religious habit until after the sixth year from the foundation of her Institute; and also that in that period of time she stayed now in the Mother House and now in another House dedicated exclusively to the schools, both existing at Piacenza. I add that in the same period of time she set about founding other houses in various places, and also went about collecting offerings for her institution.

§ 722
She exercised the office of superior with diligence and charity.
§ 723
Prudent in the admission of new Sisters.

This is what I heard said in the Community; and from the same source I learned that the Servant of God at the beginning did not put on the religious habit precisely because she had to go about to various places to develop and carry out the work that the Lord had inspired in her. After the six years the Servant of God put on the habit of her Institute and was Superior General: I do not know, however, whether she was obliged to assume that office, fixing her residence in the Mother House at Piacenza. The Servant of God exercised her office scrupulously and used much charity in directing the Sisters, joined with humility and uncommon prudence; this I know not only from report received, but also from what I myself personally experienced. To provide for the spiritual and bodily good of those under her, the Servant of God was opposed to the use of corporal penances, saying that exact observance of the common life and of the rule of the Institute sufficed, which is worth more than any penance. And only in some special case did she reluctantly permit some instrument of mortification to some individual. I recall that in the General Chapter held in 1888 in the Generalate House in Rome, there were gathered there 180 Superiors of houses for the election of the Provincials: and during the fifteen days that we were kept there, we generally admired the great patience and tirelessness of the Servant of God in listening to all of us, who had an ardent desire to receive counsel and to hear some word of hers that would serve to quiet our spirit; and there was never a case in which she refused to receive us, remaining at our disposal a great part of the day, and sometimes also in the evening until late. Many times the Secretary General, considering the weariness of the Servant of God and taking into account her frail health, would have wished that the Sisters gathered there leave the Servant of God a little free; when she learned of it, she showed displeasure and ordered the Secretary not to hinder us from going to her. Moreover, she had reserved exclusively to herself the dispatch of business and the correspondence with the Sisters of her houses in America, because she said that, since they could not hear her word by voice owing to the distance, they might have it in writing. The Servant of God was very prudent and watchful in admitting new Sisters, preferring moral and religious qualities to economic and civil ones; often, therefore, she rejected those who brought a dowry and accepted instead others who were perfectly without one, but whom she saw more adorned with virtues and suited to the ends of the Institute. The Servant of God wanted nothing necessary to be lacking to her religious: to this end she herself visited the various houses, especially at the beginning of the foundation; when afterward she appointed the Provincials, she committed to them the oversight of the proper running and of the just supply to the houses of what was necessary for life. She was also accustomed, when she heard complaints in some house, to send there a special Visitor with the obligation to report: and once I myself was called to Rome and there received an order from the Servant of God to go to one of the Houses of the Province of Como to ascertain whether the complaints coming from there were just, and to provide as need required. I recall also that whenever we went to Rome, the Servant of God, as soon as we had paid her our respects, at once dismissed us for the moment, wishing that before anything else we should refresh ourselves; and if we arrived at an hour not of the refectory, she gave the appropriate orders that fitting refreshment be promptly prepared for us, and took account of the carrying out of her orders, and this she did systematically with all our religious who came to her, as was reported to me in the community. The support of the houses, finally, was provided for as it still is, with the offerings of the faithful and with the fruit of the manifold activity of the Sisters. The Servant of God chose for the various offices those she believed suitable, without respect of persons; and in the beginning she had, in my opinion, to trust solely in God, because she was obliged to choose from the novitiate itself those who were to serve as Superiors in the various houses she opened; and in these cases she did not neglect to call the chosen ones often around her to give them wise counsels and fitting direction. The Servant of God dealt little with outsiders, except for the relations necessary by the nature of the Institute, and in the talks that she often gave us, both in common and in private, she recommended this very thing greatly, and she recommended to the Superiors to watch over their subjects in this regard, especially that they not form friendships with relatives or with little girls of the schools, or with the sick, with doctors, and in general with persons of the various administrations. The Servant of God also took great care that her religious should go decently dressed, and required uniformity in the whole habit, abhorring even the least singularity. For the sick Sisters the Servant of God provided healthful infirmaries. The first at Piacenza, a second at Naples, and a third in Sicily was begun by her; and she recommended that nothing be lacking to the sick Sisters. I can then say that the first thought of the Servant of God was to provide the religious comforts in case of need, and this too she recommended to the Superiors.

§ 725
Journeys undertaken for the good of the Institute.

Ad 18, Proc. fol. 91v.: It often happened to the Servant of God that she had to undertake journeys, whether for the opening of new houses or to visit those already founded: all the more because in the beginning of the foundation, the Provincials not yet being established in the individual centers, everything depended on the Servant of God as to the running of the Institute, and therefore she was obliged to hasten to the various houses to watch over and provide for the discipline and the life of the Congregation. Thus she had to travel nearly all of Italy, because of the many houses already opened here and there, as I have already deposed, during her life: she also went to Sicily, where her houses likewise were. As for the house opened in the Americas, the Servant of God being unable to go personally, besides having established there a Superior of her confidence, she made up for it by letters, taking information on the good running of the work and giving fitting instructions.

§ 726
Work of Perpetual Adoration of Jesus in the Sacrament.

Another work to which the Servant of God devoted herself was that of perpetual adoration of Jesus in the Sacrament. To this end she established at Piacenza a house where are gathered those among the deaf-mute girls educated by our Sisters who, having become adults, wished to remain in the Institute. To these she gave a special habit, making them perpetual adorers of Jesus in the Sacrament, whom they keep always exposed in the inner Chapel of the same House. This institution too the Servant of God made with the full assent of the local Bishop, who is its President. It is still in full life and flourishing.

§ 727
She constantly observed the law of God and of the Church.

Ad 19: The Servant of God, throughout the whole course of her life and in the various circumstances she had to face, always and constantly gave proof of most exact and exemplary observance of the law of God and of the Church, and of all her duties. As to the time before my acquaintance, and also her life before the foundation, I can depose that I always heard her spoken of as most exact and edifying in everything. Since my life with her began, I am an eyewitness of her irreproachable exactness in the observance of the holy law of God and of the Church, and of the rule of our Institute, in which she was always the first and rigorously required that it be observed by those under her. And the same I constantly heard said by my fellow Sisters who lived with the Servant of God in the various houses.

§ 728
Model of Christian life.

Ad 20: I always held the Servant of God as a true model of Christian virtues, of which she constantly gave evident proofs: and this is the opinion in which she is held generally by our Sisters and by all who knew her.

p. 477

§ 729
Living faith: devotions.

Ad 21: The Servant of God constantly gave example of a living and fervent faith. Her very life, irreproachable and edifying, is proof of the ardent faith that animated her. And to us, her daughters, she often spoke of this faith and strove to keep it alive in our hearts.

She was also most devoted to the Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ. In her room she had a beautiful image of the Crucifix, rather large, and it is common report in our Institute that before that Crucifix the Servant of God spent many hours in fervent prayer during the night; and from there she drew light and strength for her holy works. Indeed, in the most difficult circumstances, before determining to act, she used to say to us more or less thus: «Let me go a little while to take counsel with Jesus Christ» and she shut herself in her room. This image of the Crucifix, because it was so dear to the Servant of God, is kept by us with veneration in the inner Chapel of our House of Rome. She also had a small metal Crucifix which she habitually wore at her side on the bare flesh, and she pressed it so hard that it sank into the flesh, and it became, even now, soaked with her blood, as I myself saw. This is gathered from a little slip of paper found beside the same Crucifix, on which was written: This little crucifix I kept for two years close to my heart. This little crucifix too is most dear to us and is kept at Piacenza in the room inhabited by the Servant of God. The same faith made the Servant of God exceedingly zealous for the decorum of the sacred Temple, and above all for the cleanliness of the altars, on which, she said, rests the Most Holy Body of Jesus Christ: and therefore she was never sufficiently content with this cleanliness, especially in the altar cloths, the corporals, and other furnishings for the celebration of the sacred Mysteries. I, who knew thoroughly her concern for the adornment and ornament of the altars, sometimes invited her, knowing I was doing her a pleasure, to see the altar of our Chapel well prepared and clean: and she was altogether consoled by it, saying, however, that no decency or ornament was ever sufficient, since on those sacred linens the divine body of Jesus Christ was to rest. The most lively faith that the Servant of God had in the mystery of the Most Holy Eucharist made her assiduous in prayer before Jesus in the Sacrament, spending whole hours there.

I can then depose from my own knowledge, and also from what I generally heard from my fellow religious, that the Servant of God had great veneration for the Supreme Pontiff and for the Bishops, and this she always recommended to us: indeed she always told us that wherever we might be, we were to have great respect for the local Bishop, because, she said, in the individual Dioceses the Bishops take the place of the Pope and represent him. Likewise she always recommended respect for Priests.

§ 730
Her firm hope shone through her life.

Ad 22: The hope that animated her shone evidently through the life of the Servant of God. It is a fact that she despised all that the world could offer her, even the innocent joys of the family, in order to devote herself solely to God and aspire to eternal goods. And these sentiments she always instilled in us. Meditation on the last things was habitual to her, and she instilled and warmly recommended it to us; indeed she established it as a rule in our Houses every Monday.

There were not lacking occasions, especially at the beginning of the foundation, when the Servant of God found herself in straits for pecuniary means: this I in part experienced myself, but in greater part I learned from our older Sisters. And it is a fact that I know, both from my own knowledge and from the report of the said Sisters, that the Servant of God never showed herself discouraged or anxious, but fully calm and trusting in Providence, which never failed her, and sometimes even in an extraordinary way.

§ 731
Fervent divine love: preference for Jesus Crucified.

Ad 23: I am fully convinced that the Servant of God was aflame with divine love, and had by preference an immense love for Jesus Crucified, as I have already mentioned above. Her life, as far as I know, for the time in which I approached her, and from what my fellow Sisters who dealt with her more intimately than I and for longer told me and tell me, was always irreproachable and edifying, and never, as far as I know, was any voluntary fault noticed in her.

The Servant of God was much given to prayer, both vocal and mental: and as to the latter especially I wish to depose that she was always assiduous in the exercise of meditation in common in the several Houses where she was, indeed she was always the first to be in the Chapel in the morning; and it was noted with wonder and edification by all that sometimes, the Servant of God having arrived late at some House, tired from the journey, yet the next morning she rose early and was found in the Chapel at the hour of common prayer.

§ 732
Spiritual and temporal charity toward neighbor.

Ad 24: The love that the Servant of God had for the Lord also made her most charitable toward neighbor. It is a fact that her foundation is directed principally to the spiritual and temporal good of neighbor, and the various works in which it is carried out are all informed by this spirit of charity: and in this regard I refer to what I have deposed about the purpose of our Institute and the works to which we are sent by institution. I depose then, from what I know and from what my fellow religious have always told me, that the Servant of God constantly showed that she had a compassionate heart full of charity, since with all those under her she acted as a true mother, taking interest in each and every one with affection and zeal, providing according to the various needs; and this with impartiality and without respect of persons. She always recommended to those under her, especially to those at the head of the individual Houses, to attend to the individual needs of the Sisters entrusted to them, and to have charity, especially with the sick.

§ 733
The virtue of prudence.

Ad 25: Holy prudence shone constantly in the life of the Servant of God, in the way she governed herself, aiming at her own sanctification and knowing how to choose the best part, and in the irreproachable manner in which she governed the Community dependent on her. It is a fact that nothing was ever found to criticize, as far as I know, in the dispositions she issued, in the way she handled both the foundation and the running of her Institute; she always knew how to overcome all difficulties, and never gave occasion to disturbances or real dissensions among those under her. She was generally regarded by all of us as a wise and enlightened woman, and we always had recourse to her in all things, both of the work and of our individual circumstances, and we always found ourselves well in following her counsels; a word from her sufficed to dispel all doubts and resolve all difficulties. Great prudence the Servant of God always showed in correcting: she was strong and energetic, nor did she permit abuses, indeed she knew how to prevent in time any slightest disorder; but her prudence and charity brought it about that no one was offended or hurt by the correction received, since besides the gentle and winning manner with which she knew how to season the reproof, she also had the foresight to conceal, from those to whom it was not needful to reveal it, the fault or defect of the others: the correction was always made with charity and discretion and with the greatest possible secrecy.

§ 734
In the exercise of justice she was irreproachable.

Ad 26: The justice of the Servant of God was, to me, irreproachable. I have already deposed that she was most exact in her duties toward God, whose laws she faithfully observed, and whose will she respected with heroic resignation. Toward neighbor she always showed herself just, giving to each what was due. She was always submissive and respectful toward the authorities, both ecclesiastical and civil: she was always exact in compensating the services rendered to her and in giving the due wage to workmen. She was always grateful for benefits received. And these sentiments she always instilled in us, her subordinates. She was also very careful to respect and make others respect the good name of neighbor.

§ 735
Spirit of penance.

Ad 27: The life of the Servant of God was informed by rigid temperance. She always knew how to moderate her interior movements, and therefore always appeared calm and in perfect mastery of her heart and spirit: and if she sometimes had to use vehement movements to correct, she knew at once how to check these outbursts and not go beyond what was strictly necessary. She was then most mortified in the treatment of herself, however broad and generous with others, and by preference with the sick.

§ 736
Instruments of penance.

Proc. fol. 101v.: As to the spirit of mortification and penance, besides what I have already deposed, I wish to depose that the Servant of God tormented her body with special instruments. Our Sr. Serafina, who still lives in our House of Rome, told me that she, having assisted the Servant of God in her last illness, as she had also done in other earlier illnesses, a few hours before she died succeeded in removing from her loins a hairshirt which had sunk into the flesh and which was therefore soaked with blood. I do not know whether Sr. Serafina already knew of the existence of this hairshirt, being very close to and a confidante of the Servant of God and a partaker in the intimate things of her spirit, or whether she noticed it only then on touching the sick woman's side. I am convinced, however, that if she succeeded in removing the hairshirt it was only because the Servant of God, in the state to which she was reduced, perhaps did not notice it, or at least was not in a condition to prevent it.

p. 481

§ 737
Fortitude and industry; illnesses.

Ad 28: The Servant of God was during her life tormented by various infirmities, and by preference by an almost continual migraine and by an internal tremor, of which ailment she afterward died and which afflicted her for several years, but which was discovered after her death, since she, out of modesty, was always reluctant to a local medical examination. And yet the Servant of God always worked with energy and tirelessness, concealing her sufferings, and never showed herself tired or bored. Indeed she was not even accustomed to take to bed in the said circumstances of illness except in some grave case, and as soon as she could she returned to work. This in part I know from my own knowledge for the time I spent with her, and it was constantly confirmed to me by my fellow religious.

§ 738
Reserve and modesty.

Ad 29: From the whole of the life of the Servant of God there breathed a great modesty and reserve, a sure sign of the purity of her soul. In dealings she was chaste, in words measured and sober, and it is a fact that never, as far as I know, did she make mention of her life before the foundation, when she was wife and mother. Her conduct was for all of us of great edification. In the talks she gave us she would sometimes allude with much delicacy and ease to the guarding of the senses, which must be chastised to hold them in servitude, and there shone through her words the care she took to mortify herself, especially in food, to keep her senses in check.

§ 739
Model of religious poverty.

Ad 30: The Servant of God was a lover of religious poverty. In this virtue above all she was always a great example to us. She wore the same habit as ours, but always chose the roughest and most neglected: she used new clothing only rarely and when the old habit had become impossible: her linen had to be given to her and replaced at times secretly, otherwise she would never have asked for it. She always liked to go about unkempt and careless, though clean and decent.

§ 740
Example of dependence and obedience.

Ad 31: I knew the Servant of God when she was already advanced in age and Superior General of the Institute she had founded. Even so I had from her an example of dependence and obedience, since in her several Houses she wanted the local Superior to stay in her own place when she went there to stay or to visit, and to exercise equally the functions of Superior notwithstanding her presence. To us she always recommended obedience to Superiors, to Confessors, and above all to the Bishops of the places where our houses were.

§ 741
She stood out in the practice of humility.

Ad 32: An exemplary humility stood out in the life of the Servant of God. She never asked for or tolerated preferences among us on her account, fully sharing the life of a simple religious. Often she wanted to serve at table us who were under her, and sometimes she even went to the kitchen, stooping to the humblest acts. I never saw, nor heard from others, that she had haughtiness in command, but always affable, charitable and courteous manners. She treated all equally with graciousness and sweetness, even humble and common persons.

§ 742
She practiced the virtues to a heroic degree.

Ad 33: From the whole of the life of the Servant of God I formed the conviction that she, in the exercise of her virtues, reached the heroic and superlative degree, in that, as I understand, she rose above the common.

§ 743
Extraordinary gifts.

Ad 35: The Servant of God enjoyed extraordinary gifts. I was in weak health from the suffering of an ailment that prevented me from traveling, and this by the doctor's prescription. I received from the Servant of God obedience to go to several of our houses for various commissions, although the Houses indicated to me were distant from one another. I went and felt no ill. On my return I was called to Rome by telegram, and I, so as not to fail in obedience, left. As soon as the Servant of God saw me she addressed to me the following words: «You do not feel well in health, well, it is nothing, do the obedience, for you will not suffer on the journeys». And in fact the same day she let me leave for a visit to several Cities where our Houses are, namely: Florence, Modigliana, Lugo, Piacenza, and I returned to Genoa, where I was then living, and I can assure that during the journeys, in the discharge of the mission entrusted to me, I felt well. Only afterward, every commitment being finished, did I feel the ailment again, and this was verified for almost six months, the period during which my journeys lasted, and the Servant of God herself on another occasion added to me: «Do not fear, for when you grow older you will be healed», and so in fact it happened. In general, then, in our Institute I learned from other fellow religious that the Servant of God enjoyed the gift of reading hearts.

p. 483

Ad 36: The Servant of God, not knowing that I was ill with bronchitis and fever in our House of Genoa, called me another time by telegram to Rome. I, although in those conditions, so as not to fail in obedience, left for Rome. Having arrived there I presented myself to the Servant of God, concealing out of delicacy my ailment, but the Servant of God, noticing it later, ordered me to go to bed, obliging me to eat what she herself with charity had gone to prepare for me in the kitchen. I, although without appetite, ate of the meat sent by the Mother, and in the morning I rose well and healed. The Servant of God, on seeing me, said almost jestingly: «I knew you had come to Rome to eat the meat!». I held my healing to be prodigious.

§ 744
Reputation for holiness in life and after death.

Ad 43: The Servant of God enjoyed in life a reputation for holiness not only in our whole Institute, but also among outsiders who had occasion to deal with her. I, for my part, always held her as a religious of holy life. This reputation for holiness, always spontaneous, has endured after her death and has remained constant to the present. Among the outside persons who held the Servant of God in repute of holiness I can recall His Eminence Cardinal Belmonte and his family, the Princess of Fitalia of Palermo, who had much contact and trust with the Servant of God and was accustomed to consult her in matters of great importance, the Most Rev. Canon Carlo Amirante, Parish Priest of S. Maria Maggiore in Naples, previously mentioned, the late Monsignor Scalabrini, Bishop of Piacenza, and others.

§ 747
Family life and early education.

Ad 9: The Servant of God was born in Genoa on the 14th of October 1831; I do not remember the name of the father, the mother was called Adele. Her family was well-off and her parents were religious, and I, who knew the mother of the Servant of God, can affirm that she was a holy woman. She had two brothers, one Francesco, the other Federico. Three sisters, Adele, Emilia and Giustina, of whom I saw the first two a few times. All received from their parents a moral and religious education. I know that the Servant of God received at Baptism the name Rosa and that she was confirmed, as I generally heard.

Ad 10: The Servant of God had her first education in her father's house, where she also received her schooling. From infancy she showed herself of docile and benevolent disposition and showed an inclination to a life of piety and recollection, always averse to luxury and to distractions. She also showed herself a lover of charity toward the poor and the sick, especially in the Hospitals she frequented, where she went so far as to lick the sores of the sick. All this I learned generally from our Genoese Sisters, who had known the Servant of God as a child, and especially from Sr. Anna Vincenza Rapallino, who was the first Secretary of the Servant of God.

§ 748
A cultured and pious woman.

Ad 11: Besides what I have already deposed I add that the Servant of God, as I know from my own knowledge, was a cultured woman, because she wrote and spoke correctly, knew music, women's handiwork, and spoke French well, and, as I said from having heard it, as a young girl she was full of sentiments of piety toward neighbor and frequented public Hospitals to give relief to the sick.

§ 749
Model of wife, mother and Christian widow.

Ad 12: In general, from some persons of Genoa whom I cannot specify, and who were in intimate relation with the Servant of God and her family, as also from some Genoese Sisters, I learned that the Servant of God desired to consecrate her virginity to the Lord, but that afterward, to obey her parents, sure thereby of doing the will of God, she accepted to enter into marriage. She herself, the Servant of God, in some familiar talk to us Sisters repeated what I have said above. She prepared for marriage with prayers, vigils, fasts and austerities, as the aforesaid persons told me. It is notorious then that the Servant of God had three children, one whose name I do not remember and who died as a child, Alessandro, now deceased, and Carlotta, now living, both known to me.

She educated her children in a Christian way, placing the little girl Carlotta, who was deaf-mute, in a School at Milan, and she entrusted her son Alessandro to the care of a Priest. The married life of the Servant of God was full of piety and charity, as is the report among those persons who approached her, and to the religious spirit by which she always felt inspired she joined the duties of a good mother toward her children.

§ 750
Her husband having died, she thought of the foundation of the Institute.

Ad 13: After a few years of marriage the husband of the Servant of God fell ill with a long and painful illness which brought him death. The Servant of God, as I learned from the aforesaid sources, bore this tribulation resigned and was all concern in assisting her husband lovingly and with all charity. Left a widow very young with the two aforementioned children, the other having already died, as I said, she resigned herself fully to the will of Providence, and while attending to the education of her children she gave herself with greater vigor to works of piety and charity, teaching catechism to the unlettered and to peasants, visiting the Hospitals, performing lowly services for the sick who needed them, helping the poor, not neglecting her filial piety toward her parents, then still living.

Ad 14: The Servant of God, after her husband's death, felt the desire reborn to dedicate herself entirely to the Lord through the institution of a work corresponding to her ideals, always cherished by her, of doing good to neighbor.

Pious and devout as the Servant of God was, she thought she must provide herself with the counsel of enlightened persons, but I know, from having generally heard it, that the Servant of God went to Pope Pius IX, to whom she set out her desire to carry out that to which she felt inspired, that is, the foundation of an Institute having for its purpose works of charity, spiritual and corporal. She set before the Pope the anguish of her spirit over the difficulties presented to her by her parents and by the thought of the education of her children, and the Pope answered her with these words, reported to me by the Servant of God: «Rosa, follow the inspiration of God; of your children God will take care, your parents no longer have need of you. Your Institute will spread like the flight of the dove to all the corners of the earth». Comforted by the words of the Holy Father she returned to Genoa to carry out her plan, and confirmed her decision to her beloved parents. But the parents opposed it, and there are those who say that the mother of the Servant of God went so far as to stretch herself on the threshold of the house to prevent her from going out, and that the Servant of God stepped over her. Others say, as I think, that the Servant of God succeeded, with earnest entreaties, in overcoming the reluctance of her parents.
