Length of acquaintance and its motivation: The witness came to know the Servant of God at 14 (1882), when she already manifested intentions of entering religious life, but Gattorno postponed her admission for reasons of age; from January 1890, the date the postulancy began, to April 1892, the witness lived with the M. Foundress in Rome; afterward they kept frequent epistolary contacts.

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: Besides the presence of unpublished probative elements, it is evident that the witness perceived the characteristic elements of the human and spiritual story of the Servant of God. Leaving aside the news relating to the first part of her life, we present the content beginning with the analysis of how Gattorno carried out the role of Superior General of her Institute, her peculiar gifts, the esteem that surrounded her in this role. Of great importance are the proofs concerning the individual virtues, which emerge with authentic heroicity. Certainly useful, because eyewitness, are finally the pieces of information on the supernatural gifts and the reputation for holiness.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 159, testis respondit:

§ 753
General details of the witness and scope of her knowledge.

My name is Sr. Anna Cunegonda, in the world Maria Pacini, daughter of the late Giuseppe and Maria Grazia Lo Re, aged 45, born at Alessandria, Province of Girgenti, I am a professed religious of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne. At present Superior of our House of Taranto and for three months in our House of Naples, by reason of illness, and I live the common life.

Ad 7: Around my fourteenth year of age I had occasion to meet at Girgenti the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, to whom I expressed my desire to become a Sister, but the Servant of God told me to wait because I was too young. Afterward, although having a vocation to become a Sister, I began to experience a certain repugnance, thinking of the renunciation of myself that I would have to make, but, turning for this purpose by letter to the Servant of God, I always received encouraging replies, until I finally made up my mind and was admitted into the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne on 2 January 1890, in the Novitiate at Rome, and there I remained until April 1892. In that period I always saw and approached the Servant of God; then I was sent to Messina and from there to Taranto, where I am, and I have always had various occasions to approach and deal with the Servant of God.

§ 754
Foundress and vigilant superior of the Institute.

Ad 17: The Servant of God, as she was the Foundress of our Institute, was also Mother General until death, and this by the will of the Community and also of the ecclesiastical Superiors and also of the Pope. Not a few times she tried to be relieved, and I remember that when I was a novice one day the Servant of God, having gathered the whole community, in the presence of all of us knelt down begging to be relieved of her office, but the whole community did her a gentle violence that she should continue until death. The Servant of God exercised her office of Superior General with great humility, goodness, prudence and simplicity. Toward the Sisters she always showed herself a mother, providing for everything and for everyone. She was most watchful in the admission of probationers, and I remember that in the Conferences the Servant of God gave us she exhorted us to pay careful attention to the choice of young women before admitting them into the Institute. She always showed herself impartial and always assigned to the various offices those she judged the most suitable.

She never permitted the Sisters to form friendships with outsiders, especially of the other sex, and in this she showed herself most strict. She took great care that the Sisters be well housed and provided that nothing ever be lacking to them. The Community also lives on offerings and sometimes has found itself in straitened circumstances, and I remember a time when what was necessary to feed all the Sisters and the novices was lacking and the Community suddenly found itself provided for by Divine Providence.

She wished the Sisters to dress with decency and, to maintain uniformity also in the quality of the cloth to be used, she established supply stores in our Generalate House so that all the houses might be supplied. She had great concern that the sick Sisters be cared for, and for this she established proper infirmary Houses where nothing should be lacking to the sick Sisters for material assistance and also for spiritual care, and of all this she made a point of rule, so that our Sisters in case of illness are assisted according to the spirit of the Servant of God.

§ 755
Constant visits to the communities.

Ad 18: I know from my own knowledge that the Servant of God almost every year undertook journeys to visit the various Houses. I heard it said in the Community that for the same purpose the Servant of God made some journey abroad, and that sometimes, although suffering, she did not omit her journeys for visits to the various Houses, and I remember having seen her come to our House of Taranto in very poor health, and I was told that in that state the Servant of God was returning from Palermo, where she had stayed three months. I also know, from having heard it in the Community, that the Servant of God made these journeys of hers using third class on the train, but that afterward, because of her state of health, the other Sisters did her a gentle violence that she should consent to travel second class, and when she came to Taranto I saw that the Servant of God indeed stepped down from the train from a second-class carriage.

I also know, as it is notorious in the Community, that the Servant of God also founded a separate branch of Deaf-Mute Sisters, who are directed and assisted by our Sisters in Piacenza, who attend only to the adoration of Jesus in the Sacrament, and are therefore called the Adorers of Jesus in the Sacrament.

§ 756
Fidelity to the law of God and of the Church.

Ad 19: As far as I know, the Servant of God was a faithful observer of the law of God and of the precepts of the Church and of the obligations of her own state, and always zealously sought the glory of God and the spiritual good of souls.

Ad 20: The Servant of God was most observant in the exercise of the Christian virtues, Theological, Cardinal and connected, since, for the time that I knew and approached her, I always held and admired her as a holy woman and a most observant religious.

§ 757
Animated by great faith.

Ad 21: The Servant of God was animated by great theological faith, which she showed in her discourses, especially in the talks she gave us, as also in her works, always directed to honoring and giving glory to God. On all occasions she animated us to sentiments of faith toward God. Her particular concern was that God be known and loved by all, and every Sunday she wanted Jesus to be exposed in the Sacrament so that the Sisters, from 9 to 12, with special adoration by turns, might pray for the conversion of sinners and unbelievers. She wanted all the Sisters in the various houses to attend to catechetical instruction and established that such teaching be given also in the Church of our Generalate House in Rome, where I remember that when I was there as a novice more than five hundred girls of the people gathered there, and sometimes the Servant of God also took part in the teaching, and with her own hands prepared useful objects to be distributed to the girls who attended catechism, and in the repeated examinations she was always accustomed to give a prize to the most diligent to encourage them the more. I know from my own knowledge that the Servant of God was in a particular way devoted to the Most Holy Trinity, in whose honor she wrote prayers and had us Sisters practice the pious exercise of the month of January to the Eternal Father, and always inculcated in all of us such devotion. She was most devoted also to the mystery of the Nativity of Jesus, and to his Passion, and every year on Holy Thursday, Good Friday and Holy Saturday she withdrew to her little room without receiving anyone, exercising herself in penance and prayer. She had much at heart the decorum of the house of God, taking care of its cleanliness and order, and sometimes I myself saw her, not content with the work done by the Sisters assigned to the Chapel, do the cleaning herself with her own hands and require that the altars always be kept properly.

§ 758
Eucharistic life and prayer.

She approached Holy Communion with particular recollection and afterward remained a long time praying in a state as if absorbed, and when it was necessary to call her, it was necessary to shake her. Although suffering, she did not refrain from staying on her knees for long hours before Jesus in the Sacrament. I, who sometimes waited for her outside the Chapel to accompany her to visit the work of our Novitiate, said to her one day: «But what do you say, Mother, to Jesus for so long a time?», and she answered me: «Before Jesus time has no time». I then asked her to teach me to love Jesus, and she said to me: «Go, go in my presence to greet Jesus, and say to him only: Jesus, I love you; and whenever you happen to pass before him go and repeat to him the same words, and you will see that your heart will be kindled with love for him».

Finally the Servant of God cared greatly that the Lord's day be sanctified with the exercise of prayer and complete abstention from servile works, and wanted us Sisters to abstain from the smallest and slightest infraction of that obligation. She held the Word of God in great veneration and inculcated in us Sisters to read Holy Scripture and the explanations of the Gospel, and provided us for this with suitable books, and speaking to the other Superiors she exhorted them to explain the Gospel to those entrusted to them. The Servant of God always showed herself respectful of the dispositions and the authority of the Holy See and of the Bishops wherever there were houses of ours, and I remember that she recommended such obedience to us, saying that after God and the Holy Father came the authority of the Bishops, and therefore she obliged us Sisters to pay homage and make an act of obedience to the local Bishops. She loved to go to visit the Holy Father and often urged us Sisters to go on pilgrimage to the Holy Father to pay him homage.

§ 759
Animated by a great desire for eternal goods.

Ad 22: The Servant of God was animated by a great desire for eternal goods, and in her Sunday talks it was especially on the three Theological Virtues, that is, Faith, Hope and Charity, that she spoke to us. Animated by this desire she found easy and bearable the troubles and the sufferings, even physical ones, of life. Many times in her simplicity she called our attention to her sufferings, showing that she was all swollen, but at the same time full of joy, raising her eyes to heaven she exclaimed: all for my Jesus, and then repeated the words of St. Francis: So great is the good I await that every pain is a delight to me. She therefore lived detached from the things of earth and, to attend better to the salvation of her soul, chose the Religious life. In all difficulties, both for the foundation of our Institute, a certainly arduous work, and for the maintenance and development of that Institute, the Servant of God never lost her full and entire trust in God, whose Providence she therefore always experienced. Such trust, moreover, she had in everything she undertook, and therefore sought to instill it also in us Sisters. I had to suffer some aridity of spirit, and the proof of this is that, having at times had recourse to the Servant of God because I felt little fervor, she answered me: «Ah, if you only knew! Your mother too suffers from these obscurities: but one must not be discouraged, they are trials that God sends us! Even the Saints were subject to them».

p. 494

§ 760
Most virtuous life. Exercise of meditation.

Ad 23: I always admired the Servant of God for her life, in every respect most virtuous. She exercised herself much in mental prayer and in the practice of meditation. She cared greatly that the Sisters should not miss it. She always said: «Whoever does not make meditation is not saved and does not persevere in the vocation». She did not miss the common prayers, and when she was prevented by reasons of her office, she afterward went to the Chapel to make them up, and in that case always associated some other Sister with her, since she said that prayers in common have great value before God. In private, then, it is notorious in the Community that the Servant of God withdrew for a long time in prayer, and that in the afternoon after the meal she went to the Chapel where she remained long hours before Jesus in the Sacrament.

Her discourses were always inspired by holy things and things of God, and even during recreation she always took subjects from the life of some saint or also spoke of some virtue and of the way to exercise it. On every Sunday she wanted us to make acts of reparation to the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus; for this she had the Most Holy Sacrament exposed in our Church and established adoration by turns of twelve Sisters, and she herself took part in it. Out of love for Jesus in the Sacrament and to make reparation for the outrages of sinners she made the other foundation of deaf-mute Adorer Sisters of which I deposed before.

§ 761
Divine love and apostolate.

Ad 24, Proc. fol. 348v.: The Servant of God loved her neighbor in God, and to his relief consecrated all her activity. Proof of this is the foundation of our Institute, which proposes, with the glory of God, also the spiritual and temporal good of neighbor.

§ 762
She generously forgave everyone.
§ 763
Charity toward the sick.

Before founding the Institute the Servant of God already loved to devote herself to the good of neighbor. She belonged to the pious Association of the Daughters of Mary in Genoa, occupying herself especially with the spiritual good of the poor, and then also in Genoa with great love she frequented the hospitals, always seeking to be useful in helping the poor sick and the needy. And this is notorious in our Community. This love of neighbor was certainly one of the principal motives that led her to found an Institute which proposed especially the relief of the sick in private homes and in hospitals, and on the other hand to provide for the religious and civil instruction of girls and children of the people. She herself acted as teacher to the first sisters, to train them in the catechetical teaching to be given to the children of the people, and in such teaching she was always an example and encouragement to the other Sisters and recommended that it be practiced in all our houses. Many of every class had recourse to her for counsel, and the Servant of God received all with great charity. We Sisters had in the Servant of God a comfort in every anguish, a guide for every doubt of ours, and in everything recourse was always had to our Mother. Of good and charitable heart, she forgave whoever had done her an injustice: and in the Community I heard tell of a certain man, whose name I do not remember, who, enrolled in Freemasonry, for what reason I do not know, wanted to assassinate the Servant of God, waiting hidden to attack her. Which he did not succeed in doing, because the Servant of God passed before him unnoticed, not without prodigy, in our common judgment. The Servant of God not only forgave him but even had prayers said in the Community for his conversion. The Servant of God had great compassion for the souls in Purgatory and inculcated in all of us devotion to those souls, establishing appropriate general practices for the whole community: especially on the occasion of the death of some fellow Sister, Masses must be applied for the deceased sister and by all the Sisters prayers and Holy Communion be offered in suffrage. When I was at Girgenti as a boarding student, the Servant of God came to visit that House of ours, and I remember that she did not wish to leave without having visited the local Hospital, though not staffed by her Sisters, so imperious in her heart was the sentiment of charity for her sufferers; so she called the sick. It was above all this sentiment of compassion for the sick that decided her to give us Sisters no other title than that of Nursing Sisters. She taught us the way to help the poor sick and suggested that we greet the sick on approaching them, since she said: «You greet Jesus Christ in the sick person». Besides this great compassion for the sick, she had no dissimilar feeling for other human misfortunes, and busied herself especially in relieving the poor in their needs, for whom she herself made handiwork which she distributed to them. She provided a safe refuge for orphans: she established orphanages at Piacenza, Lodi, Foligno, in Sampierdarena, where many poor girls, assisted by our Sisters, find food, shelter and religious and civil education until the age of majority.

§ 764
Superior full of prudence.

Ad 25: The Servant of God in the exercise of Superior General showed that she possessed great prudence, especially in the assignment of the Sisters to the various offices of our Institute. I always availed myself of the counsels of the Servant of God and found myself content, and in general I know that all those who turned to the Mother remained satisfied from carrying out her counsels. Among those who habitually availed themselves of the counsels of the Servant of God were the Prince and Princess of Fitalia of Palermo. She was grieved at the failings of some fellow Sister, and provided prudently that the bad example not spread and, at the opportune time, therefore, she with all prudence sought to correct the abuses and the failing Sisters.

§ 765
Spirit of mortification and instruments of penance.

Ad 27: The Servant of God lived a most mortified life, chose for herself the poorest and vilest things and shunned everything pleasant. She was very mortified in food; for the time I was in Rome and also in Naples, in the refectory, I never saw the Servant of God eat meat. Ordinarily she fed on vegetables with oil or boiled potatoes and sometimes a little fish. At her place I never saw wine; instead she drank only water. In the Community it was the general conviction that the Servant of God did this out of mortification. She slept on a straw mattress without sheets and only covered with a blanket; the pillow too was of straw, as I had occasion to ascertain personally, having gone some times to look for the Servant of God in her bedroom. She slept little, and when the Community gathered in the Chapel for the morning prayers I already saw the Servant of God there, recollected in prayer; and then it was known from her Secretaries that the Servant of God spent a great part of the night in prayer. It is notorious in our Community that the Servant of God used instruments of penance and that in our house at Piacenza there is a room where the Servant of God used to retire often to discipline herself and do other penances. Therefore in that room there are still preserved hairshirts, disciplines, sandals with spikes and other things, all instruments of penance said to have been used by the Servant of God. Among the other things preserved are two large crosses where it seems the Servant of God stretched herself, and also a small Crucifix which, as I was told in the Community, the Servant of God wore for seven years tightly pressed over the heart, until a purulent sore formed at that point. I can attest only that, having had in my hands shirts of the Servant of God, I saw traces of matter precisely on the side of the heart and also stains of rust around. Of that Crucifix the Servant of God deprived herself by obedience to her Confessor, as was found written in her own hand on a sheet in which the same Crucifix was wrapped.

From Sr. Anna Serafina, now residing in Rome, I was told that the Servant of God, near death, gave her an order to remove from her an iron belt with which she was girded, but that, through long use, it had penetrated into the body and the said Sister had to use pincers, with which she succeeded in tearing off only a piece.

§ 766
Fortitude in the difficulties of the foundation.

Ad 28: The foundation of our Institute was certainly accompanied by no slight difficulties. First of all, the Servant of God had the opposition of her mother, who decidedly did not want to be deprived of her, her daughter, but the Servant of God, feeling imperious in her heart the call of God, sacrificed this affection of hers also. Afterward financial difficulties were added, the enterprise becoming arduous in its development, as well as other contrarieties in general which always accompany the works of God; but the Servant of God, as far as I know, also because it is notorious in the Community, never lost her tranquility of spirit and faced everything with Christian fortitude and, with the help of God, triumphed over every difficulty. Moreover I can depose that the Servant of God was always ailing in health, but she, with her habitual smile, concealed her sufferings, which she always bore with resignation; not only that, but even while suffering she always worked at the direction of our Institute in her capacity of Superior General.

§ 767
Love and practice of chastity.

Ad 29: The Servant of God, as far as I know personally, greatly loved the virtue of chastity, since she strove with her discourses and counsels to arouse in us Sisters such love. For the rest, I can affirm that her conduct was always in every respect reserved; above all when she had to approach, by reason of office, persons of the other sex, she did so with such dignity and reserve that I, who was sometimes present in the guest parlor, was filled with great admiration. Her discourses were always inspired by holy things, never vain and idle, and in her whole bearing one clearly saw the virtuous woman.

§ 768
Model of religious poverty.

Ad 30: The Servant of God, as I know from my own knowledge, dressed very poorly, in habits that were clean but patched, and took her delight when she could wear something that others had put out of use. In her room I never saw anything refined; a straw mattress, two chairs, a common straw prie-dieu formed all the furniture of her room. She sought to instill such love of poverty in us Sisters; therefore she made her remonstrances if any had chosen a certain elegance in her habit, and even required that we use common glass buttons and not bone ones, since she used to say: St. Anne wants us to be poor, so we must use what costs least.

§ 769
She greatly loved the virtue of humility.

Ad 31: I refer to what I have deposed and add that the Servant of God always inculcated in us the virtue of obedience to our Superiors. The Servant of God had the virtue of humility greatly at heart. Already at the first dealing with her one saw the humility of her manners, of her speaking and of her thinking. She esteemed herself the last among all and believed herself good for nothing. She did not want to be called Foundress or Mother General; the Foundress, she said, is St. Anne, I am nothing but a vile instrument, and in the General Chapter she begged the assembled Sisters to dispense her from the office of Superior General. She always said she knew how to do nothing, though having culture and succeeding at everything: indeed I remember that once, taking from my hands an embroidery work that I was doing, she began with her own hand to spoil it, just to be thought inept. Of this virtue the Servant of God was a teacher to us Sisters, not only with words, but especially with her example.

§ 770
She attained heroism in the practice of virtue.

Ad 33: From the whole life of the Servant of God, which was in every respect constantly virtuous and exemplary, I depose that she, in the exercise of the Christian virtues, attained heroism, since she exercised them not in a common and ordinary way, but in an extraordinary and superlative way, so as to surpass in short the common run of other souls, even pious and virtuous, which means in a heroic degree, as I understand.

§ 771
She practiced the virtues without exaggeration.

Ad 34: I have never heard, known or read that the Servant of God, in the exercise of the Christian virtues, ever fell into some excess of exaggeration or made herself less fit for the fulfillment of her office; indeed I can depose from my own knowledge that the Servant of God worked until death and that barely two days before dying she wished to attend a clothing of Sisters in spite of her grave sufferings.

pp. 499–500

§ 772
Extraordinary gifts.

Ad 35: The Servant of God was enriched by the Lord with extraordinary gifts. To a young lady whose name I do not remember, who asked to become a sister, the Servant of God said to think it over well, since hers was not a vocation but a mere desire; in fact, the said young lady insisting, she became a Sister, but after not even a month the community was obliged to send her home. I remember that Sister by the name of Sr. Anna of St. Ignatius; I know that she went back to the world but I do not know where she is at present. To me myself, who during the Exercises of preparation for the Clothing was seized by temptation and wanted to withdraw, the Servant of God showed that she would satisfy me at once, saying that she would telegraph my family, and meanwhile had me leave the Exercises. Several times in the day I asked whether an answer had come from my home, persisting in my idea, but toward evening, I do not know how, I felt tranquil and with a peace in my heart, and then I went to ask the Servant of God to grant me the habit. The Servant of God, with a good-natured smile: «I knew», she answered me, «that it was a temptation; besides, I have not yet telegraphed your home, and see there, beautiful and ready, the habit you are to put on», and so the next day I clothed myself as a Sister. In the year 1891, in the General house in Rome, on the 15th of December, the Servant of God had me called to her room and, on seeing me, invited me to make prayers to the Child Jesus with her, and so saying she added: «I want to show you something», and drew from a wall niche a Child, I do not know whether of wood or of other material, in appearance as if covered with bruises, so that I touched it, they seeming to me stains. But the Servant of God smiled and said: «No, daughter, it is Jesus who suffers for the sins of our Sisters»; I then felt great impression and almost horror at looking at that Child, and the Servant of God, encouraging me, added: «Will you help me to pray to the Child Jesus?». I assented, and the Servant of God, setting the Child on a small table that served her as a writing desk, knelt beside me and together we made prayers, when suddenly the Servant of God speaks no more, and remains motionless with her gaze fixed on high while tears ran down from her eyes and her head was as if shaken by shudders, almost showing repugnance. I then shook the Servant of God repeated times, since I began to be afraid, but the Servant of God did not stir and remained in that attitude for almost three quarters of an hour. Having come to herself: «I charge you», she said, «not to tell anyone what you have seen; indeed you must swear to me that not even after my death will you disclose it, even if our Cardinal Protector should question you». I swore to her and have kept the oath until this moment. During this novena of Holy Christmas the Servant of God also said to me: «We must do some penance to make reparation for the offenses done to Jesus». On the 24th of the same month the Servant of God invited me again to her room and showed me that same child, but oh how different! he was so beautiful and radiant that I felt rapt, and the Servant of God said to me: «See, there in the Americas some of our Sisters were displeasing Jesus because they wanted to make a schism». And I asked her what this schism is, and the Servant of God answered: «They wanted to desert our Institute for a foundation contrary to ours». I added: «But how did you come to know it?», and the Servant of God answered me: «Jesus sent me there; everything has been arranged, only one had to leave, and it was fitting that she leave». After these events some months passed and it became known in the Community that in our House in America the Servant of God was seen, in the month indicated.

It was 1890, in our house in Rome, and I was among the novices. One day, it was a Thursday, about 10 o'clock, the Servant of God having sent out on an errand, perhaps our Mistress, she turned to us saying: «I have come to stay a little while with you, well, what do you want me to tell you?», and we all in chorus: Mother, we said to her, speak to us a little of the love of God. The Servant of God protested that only the Seraphim could speak of the love of God, but nevertheless she began to be seized and carried away by it, and so she spoke with ardor, standing in the place where our Mistress used to stand, on a small dais, with a small bare table before her. Continuing in her discourse she became so eloquent and aflame that all of us were enchanted and hung on her lips, which dizzyingly articulated words of Paradise. Suddenly a companion near me called my attention, showing me the Servant of God raised above the said dais; indeed, stretching out her hand, she measured the distance between the soles of the Servant of God's feet and the dais and ascertained that she was held raised from the ground to a height of about four fingers. The news spread instantly among all the novices, almost ninety in number, and all, amazed, began to look, and then, seized with great emotion, we all fell on our knees and, weeping, remained contemplating the Servant of God, who lasted in that attitude, raised, for almost half an hour. The companion who called my attention seems to me to have been, I do not remember whether Sr. Gualberta, now deceased, or Sr. A. Domenichina, whom I do not know in which of our Houses she is at present. Among the novices present at the event I recall Sr. A. Odilia, Sr. A. Olimpia, Sr. A. Gasperina, Sr. A. Rosalia, Sr. A. of Santa Margherita, Sr. A. of St. Raphael, Sr. A. Nazzarena Zuccarà and others whom I cannot specify at the moment.

§ 773
Reputation for holiness in life and after death.

Ad 43: In our Community and outside it, among all who approached her, the Servant of God always enjoyed a reputation for holiness, both in life and after death. In this reputation for holiness the Servant of God was held also by eminent persons, among whom I can cite Card. Verga, Card. Alimonda, Card. Sanfelice, from whom I heard the Servant of God spoken of as a saint. Cardinal Guarino, Archbishop of Messina, said to me one day: «Your Institute goes forward because you have a Saint at its head», alluding to the Servant of God. The Bishop of Girgenti, Monsignor Blandini, on coming to greet the Servant of God, knelt before her in the act of kissing her hand, and the Servant of God, still more swiftly, prostrated herself at the feet of the said Bishop, declaring herself a wretched creature, and then that Monsignor rose and, holding out his hand to the Servant of God, helped her to rise. At this meeting I was present, together with our Sisters and the pupils, in our House of Girgenti. Such a reputation for holiness, entirely spontaneous in view of the singular virtues of the Servant of God, endures uninterrupted and has become more firmly established after her death. I, for my part, have always held and hold the Servant of God to be a great saint.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 170v., testis respondit:

My name is Sr. Anna Ulderica Tazzioli, in the world Maria, daughter of the late

§ 774
General details of the witness.

Giovanni Battista and Marianna Canove, born at Montefiorini, Province of Modena, on the 11th of April 1862; I am a Religious of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne; I am at present Superior of our House of Ortona a Mare, where I reside and live the common life, and I am passing through Naples.

Ad 7: I was educated by the Sisters of St. Anne and from then on I heard the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno spoken of with praise by those same Sisters. Afterward, at the age of fifteen, I entered as a postulant the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne at Piacenza, then the Generalate House, and there I came to know the Servant of God personally and lived there three years. Assigned afterward elsewhere, on several occasions I had opportunity to see and to approach the Servant of God. I shall therefore say what I know personally in conscience and what I have been able to hear from others.

§ 775
She founded the Institute with the sole purpose of charity.

Ad 16: I have already deposed that the Servant of God in the foundation had no other purpose than that of charity, and the first House I do not remember well whether it was at Piacenza or at Sampierdarena. When I entered, in 1877, the Institute already counted three hundred Sisters, and at present there are many thousands. While the Servant of God was still living, several Houses were opened in Italy and also abroad, especially in the Americas, and after her death they multiplied more and more, so that the Institute has had a vast increase. In the Institute simple vows of poverty, chastity and obedience are made, to which in the beginning was added that of assistance to the sick, which afterward the Servant of God herself prudently thought it right to suppress, seeing by experience that not all the Sisters could submit to it. These vows are renewed every year and after a decade one may ask to be admitted to perpetual vows. I remember that the Servant of God joined us in the annual renewal of vows. Those who had made them perpetual renew them in spirit.

§ 776
Prudent superior full of charity.

Ad 17: Since I entered the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, I found the Servant of God Superior General of it, and such she was until death. I have heard it said generally in the Community that to elect and confirm her in this office the general vote of the Sisters concurred and, as they told me, also the express will of the Supreme Pontiff Pius IX. They also reported to me that the Servant of God, out of humility, several times asked to be relieved of this office, but her resignation was never accepted. It is a fact, then, which I know in part from my own knowledge, in part from what I always heard in the Community, that she had the gifts of an excellent Superior. She knew how to uphold with decorum the principle of authority, without descending to weakness and without producing abuses or laxity; but at the same time she knew how to govern with humility, charity and sweetness, making herself loved more than feared. She was most prudent in government in general; but principally most watchful in admitting new members into the Institute: shrewd in the choice, most attentive in the time of postulancy or probation, testing well the spirit and vocation of each. At the same time she kept her eye on discerning the aptitude and capacity of each, and when need arose she knew how to assign suitable Sisters to the individual offices; it is a fact that all those chosen by her gave excellent proof. The Servant of God was then a true mother in her Institute, providing for all the needs of those under her, both in the spiritual and in the temporal part. She was solicitous that the Sisters should have suitable confessors and did not let preaching and religious instruction fail: she took care that nothing necessary be lacking for food and the other needs of the houses and of the individual Sisters. And I remember that for the Houses where she could not be personally present she used to say to the Sisters that if ever the local Superior let anything be lacking, they should write at once to her, and she would provide. She was always most watchful, indeed strict, in not permitting the Sisters relations with outside persons, outside the case of real necessity, and in this regard at times she gave proof of great energy, preventing, punishing, and also changing the residence of the Sister who had given sign of some levity in this matter. She used to inspect well the premises where she planted branches of her Institute, nor did she permit the opening unless beforehand, by her own eyes or through competent persons, she had assured herself of the suitability of the place and the house, both on the hygienic side and on the moral side. She was also exact in requiring of those under her that they dress and conduct themselves decently. As to the means for the upkeep of the Institute and of the works, at the beginning of the foundation the Servant of God provided primarily with her own means, being of a rather well-off family, and with the alms collection she made, especially for the upkeep of the orphanage she founded. Afterward, as the Institute developed further, the means were and are supplied by the proceeds obtained from the very works carried out, that is, assistance in the schools, in the Hospitals, to private sick persons and similar works.

The Servant of God had an extraordinary charity toward the sick members of our Institute: she provided a suitable infirmary in the principal houses, furnishing it with everything needed for the sick, and for the spiritual part she especially wanted the assistance of a Priest and ease of frequenting the Sacraments. But it is a fact that in all the Houses the local sick are cared for with charity and maternal assistance by special provisions established in our rules.

§ 777
She frequently visited the communities to provide for the good of the Institute.

Ad 18: The Servant of God, as far as I know, partly from my own knowledge and partly from what our Sisters told me, was almost continually traveling to provide directly for the good of her Institute. She went for the most part personally to the places where new houses were to be opened or branches of the work installed: every year she wanted to visit each of the houses scattered through the various cities of Italy, and there she listened to each of the Sisters and saw with her own eyes the needs. For these journeys she used the means according to the circumstances of the places, either trains, or carriages, or mounts, or boats at sea, she used what was strictly necessary, without regard for comfort and still less for luxury. It is known that the Servant of God suffered greatly in traveling by carriage, and still more in going by sea; and yet she did not spare herself when it was a matter of the good of the Institute. I myself have sometimes seen that she arrived in Sicily in a state to arouse pity from the seasickness suffered; and yet as soon as she had recovered with a brief rest, she set to work and attended to everything and everyone, not caring for herself. As for the foreign houses, especially of America, being unable to go there personally, the Servant of God provided by letters and through the Provincials or special delegates. I know of the existence at Piacenza of a house of deaf-mute sisters who wear more or less the same habit as ours and are called the Minims of St. Anne: they have as Superior one of our Sisters, and our Sisters also are the teachers and the other officers. The deaf-mute Sisters are assigned to the perpetual adoration of Jesus in the Sacrament. I could not say precisely whether these were founded on the initiative of the Servant of God: it is certain, however, that she had a great part in it.

§ 778
Reputation for holiness. Exemplary life.

Ad 19: I depose with full conviction, from what I saw and from what I learned in the community and outside, that the Servant of God was most exact, throughout the whole course of her life, in the observance of the precepts of God and of the Church and of the obligations of her state, and of the vows made. Her life was most exemplary and edifying.

Ad 20: From what I myself had occasion to admire in the conduct of the Servant of God during the time I approached her, and from what I have constantly heard and hear in praise of her, I have a great idea of her truly virtuous life, which, in my judgment, possessed all the virtues and exercised them until death.

WITNESS VIII
Sr. ANNA APOLLONIA MARCHETTI

Scope in the process: From Sess. 17th of 26 May 1913 (fol. 191v.) to Sess. 21st of 18 November 1913 (fol. 228).

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Giuseppina Marchetti, born in 1851 at Vaccari (Piacenza).

p. 506

State and profession: Religious of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, now retired.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness when she came to know the Servant of God: about 17 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness came to know her: about 37 years.

Age of the witness at the time of the deposition: 62 years.

Length of acquaintance and its motivation: The witness came to know the Servant of God in 1868-1869 at Piacenza; there she lived beside the Foundress for about 7 years, the first of her religious life; afterward she met her several times as opportunity allowed.

Observations on the witness, on the scope and on the content of the deposition: The contribution supplied by the present witness is significant both for its content and for the extent of the proofs, with information on the first years of the life of the Servant of God, the marriage period, the years of widowhood marked by great activity. The witness offers a good contribution on the way the Servant of God directed the Institute and on the heroic exercise of the virtues. This theme is treated so broadly and in such detail that the omission of some passages was necessary. For the same reasons of brevity we had to eliminate the narration of supernatural gifts.

The reputation for holiness enjoyed by the Servant of God in life and after death emerges very clearly.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 192, testis respondit:

§ 779
General details of the witness and scope of her knowledge.

My name is Sr. Apollonia, in the world Giuseppina Marchetti, daughter of Pietro and Luigia Donati, born at Vaccari, province of Piacenza, aged 62; I am a professed Religious of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, I have been Superior in various of our Houses and at present, by reason of infirmity, I am at Naples in our House at Villa St. Anne at Ottocalli, where I live the common life.

Ad 7: I came to know the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno personally around 1868-69, when I asked to be admitted to the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne at Piacenza. I was received with great rejoicing by the Servant of God, and I was captivated by her amiability and within a few days I made my entrance into the Institute. The first seven years I spent in our House at Piacenza, where the Servant of God habitually lived. Afterward I always saw the Servant of God again as opportunity allowed, finding myself in other houses. I always had of the Servant of God the impression of a religious by no means ordinary, who attracted by her uncommon virtues.

§ 780
Family and early education.

Ad 9: The Servant of God was born in Genoa around 1831; I do not remember the name of the father; I knew the mother, named Adelaide, who was a holy woman. I know, having known them, two brothers of the Servant of God, Francesco and Federico, and two sisters, Giustina and the other Elvira, as I recall; I do not know whether all are living. The parents educated their children in the Christian way, and I know that the Servant of God received in baptism the name of Rosa. Being with the said Signora Adelaide, mother of the Servant of God, as a nurse, around 1874-75, in Genoa, Signora Adelaide told me that, having been visited by Pius IX before he was Pope, he, seeing the Servant of God as a little child, said to her mother: take care of this creature, who will have to come to me several times; and so it came about.

Ad 10: Conversing sometimes with the Servant of God, I learned that she had her education in her family. From Signora Adelaide, mother of the Servant of God, I learned that from childhood she always showed herself docile, obedient and a lover of piety, so much so that she always wished to go to church.

Ad 11: From the said Signora Adelaide it was reported to me that the Servant of God was always obedient to her and that whatever she could gather at home she distributed to the poor. She frequented the work of the Hospital in company with a Lady named Giustina. She had sufficient culture and was trained in women's work and in every other domestic task, so much so that she acted as teacher to the first Sisters who gathered in the Institute under her dependence and direction.

§ 781
Marriage and married life: fortitude and serenity.

Ad 12: From the same said Signora Adelaide I learned that the Servant of God entered marriage solely by the will of her parents: she having shown a desire to become a religious, but the parents opposing it, the father said to her, to persuade her to marriage: «You will become a nun at 33».

I knew personally two children of the Servant of God, Carlotta and Alessandro, called by us Sisters «Gigino». The son Alessandro was kept by the Servant of God in a school run by religious, and Carlotta always made her Communion every day with us Sisters, after her 15th year. Previously, being deaf-mute, she had been also in a school for the deaf-mute, where she was educated. Even when married, the Servant of God did not leave the work of the hospitals, which she frequented with all charity and zeal.

Ad 13: From the mother of the Servant of God I learned that she, having had a choleric husband, was likewise always resigned, patient and lovingly assisted him until the last hour of his life. From my sister Maria Marchetti I was then informed that on the occasion of the death of Mr. Alessandro, son of the Servant of God, she assisted him lovingly and wished personally to keep vigil beside him to lavish on him all care, and when death had occurred she showed herself strong and resigned.

§ 782
First idea of the foundation of the Institute.

Ad 14: The Servant of God always desired a state of perfection; therefore she bore the married state because it was imposed on her by her father, as I have already deposed. When her husband died, the Servant of God sought at once to put her desires into effect and, inspired to make a new foundation, she took counsel with the Archbishop of Genoa, who, not wishing to lose the charitable activity that the Servant of God displayed in Genoa, showed himself little favorable. The Servant of God then turned to the Bishop of Acqui, who did not want new religious foundations in his Diocese, as I learned afterward from his successor Bishop. The Servant of God then, to know more surely the will of God, presented herself to Pope Pius IX, who received her kindly and said to her: «Put your hand to the work, for you will be blessed by God». So it was reported to me by the late Canon Cogrossi of Piacenza.

§ 783
Beginning of the Institute: meeting with Pius IX.

Ad 15: The Servant of God, as I learned generally at Piacenza, my native place, met in Rome, after having visited Pope Pius IX, a canon of Piacenza, the above-named Cogrossi, who, also having the intention of founding a new Institution, encouraged the Servant of God to go to Piacenza, assuring her that she would find the favor of the local Bishop, who desired in his Diocese an Institute of charity. The Servant of God consented and, having come together to Piacenza, they negotiated the purchase of Casa Verme, where the Servant of God withdrew in company with three other Genoese ladies, Mrs. Rocco Elisa and two others whose names I do not remember. Soon the Servant of God, together with her companions, began to gather endangered young girls to educate them and to assist the poor sick in their homes, and this was the purpose the Institute founded by her afterward had; but in the City they were then known under the name of Genoese Ladies. Meanwhile the Servant of God had already provided for the education of her children, placing them respectively in School, as I have already deposed.

§ 784
Title of the Institute: rules and approval.

Ad 16: When I entered the Institute it was already called that of the Daughters of St. Anne, and I put on the habit we have at present. However, at the beginning of the foundation the Institute was entitled that of the Daughters of the Immaculate, with a variation in the habit we wear at present, since the first ones used especially a transparent silk veil on the head. From my novice mistress, who was Sr. Eufemia, I learned that St. Anne had appeared to the Servant of God and had revealed to her that she wanted the Institute under her protection and the habit reformed as we have it at present. I can depose, as I know, that the Institute founded by the Servant of God made rapid progress; in fact I, who entered the Institute barely three years after the foundation, found already three houses open: that of Piacenza, which was the first, the second at Cento and the third at Sampierdarena. The first houses having been founded, the Servant of God personally dictated the norms for the Sisters, norms which afterward were drawn up in the form of a rule and submitted to the approval of ecclesiastical authority. Finally, while the Servant of God was still living, the Rules were approved by the Holy See with some modification. In the Institute the vows of Poverty, Chastity and Obedience are made. The Servant of God had added a fourth vow, assistance to the sick at home or in Hospitals, of both sexes, of whatever condition and whatever infirmity, a vow which was suppressed by the Holy See, judged useless because included in that of obedience.

These vows, for the first ten years, are renewed every year, and after the ten years one may be admitted to perpetual vows, at the judgment of the Superiors. The Servant of God, at the beginning of the foundation, did not take the Religious habit at once, in my judgment in order to be freer to settle her affairs, but she lived nevertheless in Community dressed in lay clothes, and after about a year she took the Religious habit and together with the first Sisters made the said vows. While the Servant of God was still living, the Institute had great increase and I remember that at the first Chapter held at Piacenza 180 Superiors took part, the Servant of God included, and at the second Chapter held in Rome, since I was then a Superior, we were 315 at the Tabella. After the death of the Servant of God the Houses have grown still more in number.

§ 785
Superior general: prudent and solicitous government.

Ad 17: The Servant of God, having founded our Institute, was in fact its Superior General. Several times she showed a desire to leave her office, but with the unanimous vote of us other Sisters she was always confirmed and held the office of Superior General until death. In this regard I remember that the Servant of God wished to resign from her office in order to go to America as a simple Sister, and we Sisters insisted strongly that she remain, thereby obtaining the consent of the Bishop, who had earlier shown himself inclined to the desire of the Servant of God. In the repeated confirmations there was, however, the consent of the Bishop of Piacenza, where the first Generalate House was; and later, the Institute having had greater increase, in the confirmation of the Servant of God as Superior General there was also the consent of Pope Pius IX of holy memory.

The Servant of God discharged her office with great zeal and charity, was always amiable with the Sisters under her, and if at times she had to correct someone she did so with great charity. It never happened that she rebuked a Sister in public; at the moment she made a sign of reproof, but she always reserved the right to call the faulty Sisters aside and give them charitable admonitions.

She was most prudent in admitting postulants; from me she required all the appropriate documents for my entrance into the Institute, even requiring the document of freedom before the Civil registry, not excluding the medical examination when she thought it fitting.

She was solicitous not to let the necessary sustenance fail the Sisters, providing for what they needed. She never showed partiality and always assigned to the offices those Sisters whom before God she judged most suitable. She forbade the Sisters, outside of necessity, conversation with outside persons. She also took care to keep the Sisters always in decent and airy Houses, as they now exist in the various cities of Italy, which I have largely traveled.

The House we have at Sampierdarena was part of the patrimony of the Servant of God and was ceded by her to the Institute; at her own expense she acquired the House at Piacenza and built from the foundations the one at Rome. For the other Houses she provided also with the help of benefactors. She provided the Institute with proper Infirmaries, never letting the Sisters lack the appropriate aid in their various infirmities, and she took special care that spiritual aid not be lacking in grave cases. When she noticed that a Sister did not approach Holy Communion she called her aside and, without investigating the reason, asked only whether it would please her to go to some other confessor; and at times she had us go out, giving us the opportunity to confess elsewhere in order to safeguard freedom of conscience. Finally, she wanted the Sisters to dress decently and in a uniform habit.

§ 786
She spared no hardship to visit the communities.

Ad 18: The Servant of God used each year to visit almost all the Houses in Italy, alternating the years for the Houses in Sicily; as I recall she visited also twice the Houses in France, and notwithstanding her unsteady health she spared no hardship to fulfill this duty of hers as Superior General, and ordinarily she arrived unexpected, without notice. This she did up to a year before her death. At Legnano there was a refuge for deaf-mute girls who were employed in manual work, assisted by our Sisters.

On the death of their benefactor, the Servant of God, so as not to leave those poor girls without a guide, some of whom also desired to become Religious, established, some ten years before her death, a special Institute of deaf-mutes with the title: Daughters of St. Anne Adorers of the Most Blessed Sacrament, an institution still in force, forming a branch of our Institute. In this the Servant of God was in agreement with Monsignor Scalabrini, the late Bishop of Piacenza, who took the place of the deceased benefactor for those girls.

§ 787
Model of all the virtues until death.

Ad 19: For the time I knew the Servant of God and from what I heard from her own mother I can depose that the Servant of God was a faithful observer of the precepts of God and of the Church and of the duties of her own state until her death; and she always zealously sought the glory of God and the salvation of souls.

She was always ready to run where there was need of help; and in this regard I remember that, when I was in our House at Piacenza, one evening at a late hour the Servant of God, hearing a groan coming from the street, noticed the presence of a soldier left wounded on a sidewalk by the troops who had passed there on their way to maneuvers. The Servant of God ran at once and, assisted by some Sisters, gave that wounded man first aid, using for the urgency of the case her handkerchief to make a bandage.

Ad 20: The Servant of God, as I know, exactly practiced all the Christian virtues, none excepted, and until her death. For us Sisters she was always a model of observance and of virtue, and her presence alone was already for us an incentive to the practice of virtue and to the observance of our Rules.

§ 788
Active and living faith.

Ad 21: The Servant of God, as I know, was animated by true theological faith, which was her guide in the fulfillment of the precepts of God and of the Church and of the obligations of her own state. Such faith she showed also in her discourses, which were always inspired by holy things and by incitements to the exercise of virtue. She personally busied herself with the instruction of children of both sexes and exhorted us Sisters to do likewise. She gave us Sisters conferences and instructions on the mysteries of the faith and on the truths of our Religion, educating us personally in the practice of Meditation, and I still remember all the beautiful maxims she suggested to us.

§ 789
Devotions, expressions of faith.

She was most devoted to the mystery of the Incarnation and, to solemnize the Nativity of Jesus Christ, asked for and obtained permission to have the three Masses celebrated at midnight so that we Sisters could with all devotion approach the Sacred Table together with her at that solemn hour, and the little girls sheltered by us also took part in the service.

She was most devoted to Jesus Crucified, of whom she lovingly kept an image, and in the Community the word was spread that the Crucifix spoke to the Servant of God. We saw that before any undertaking the Servant of God recollected herself in prayer in her room, and once she stayed there three days and was seen only at Communion and at the other practices of piety usually done in common. She performed with us of the Community the pious practice of the Sacred Heart and proposed, without imposing, some abstinence on all Fridays, and she placed in the Rules abstinence from fruit on the first Friday of every month.

Most loving of Jesus in the Sacrament, she fostered perpetual adoration and I remember that in our House at Piacenza she never left Jesus in the Sacrament alone and established for this purpose a turn of adoration that began at 5:15 in the morning, and for the first two hours the adoration was made by two Sisters without alternation, and from 7:15 it alternated hour by hour until 9 in the evening. This turn was always kept by two Sisters and four pupils of the Orphanage kept by us. Because of her devotion to the Most Blessed Sacrament she wanted her other Institution of the Deaf-mutes, of which I have already spoken, to take the title of Perpetual Adorers of the Most Blessed Sacrament, and in fact that Institute is in full vigor and those Sisters give themselves to the adoration of the Most Blessed Sacrament.

She received Communion every day with great devotion and deep recollection, so much that she remained motionless and in ecstasy for some time. In her little room at Piacenza she had a small window that opened onto the Church, where she remained in prayer before the Most Blessed Sacrament, as I happened to observe several times at night when going to the Church out of necessity.

§ 790
Theological hope.

Ad 22, Proc. fol. 201v.: Concerning Christian Hope I depose that the life of the Servant of God was informed by virtue to such a degree as to show that she always thought of the attainment of eternal salvation and of the means to arrive at it. She took no account of temporal things, from which she lived entirely detached, and I can say that in everything there was contempt of herself. She never kept anything special for herself and took exclusively from the Community the bare necessity; indeed we Sisters were obliged to change her habits or other effects always secretly, because the Servant of God did not want new habits.

The exemplary character of her life is proof that the Servant of God embraced the Religious state by divine vocation and attended to the Foundation of the Institute for the sole glory of God. The difficulty of the enterprise appears all the greater if one considers that she attended to the Foundation of the Institute in times of political upheaval, when Cloisters and Convents were arbitrarily being closed. In any temporal distress the Servant of God showed herself always confident in divine Providence. On the occasion when a fire broke out in the chimneys of our House at Piacenza, the Servant of God, having the alarm given, ran to pray in our Chapel before the Altar of St. Joseph and, among the many who came running, an unknown gentleman was seen, who, climbing onto the roof, using barely two buckets of water and having the chimney closed below with a woolen blanket well soaked in water, put out the fire that threatened the whole House, and immediately no one noticed where he had withdrawn to. I, charged by the Servant of God to thank that gentleman, no longer found him, nor was he seen by others. I expressed my wonder at it to the Servant of God, who said: «Go and thank St. Joseph, because he saved us».

§ 791
Love of God, living Rule of piety and virtue.

Ad 23: The Servant of God was filled with divine love, her life was most exemplary both in the world, as her mother and the aforementioned maid Maddalena reported to me, and afterward in Religion, as I was able to observe personally for all the time I approached her; and for us Sisters she was a living Rule of piety and virtue. Her will was always conformed to the will of God, as she showed by her discourses always inspired by holy things, by the exercise of mental prayer, and in this she was a teacher to us to train us in this pious exercise, and by the fervor with which she approached Holy Communion.

Finally, she grieved at the thought of the offense against God and said she could not persuade herself how a Christian soul could reach such excess.

§ 792
Various manifestations of charity toward neighbor.

Ad 24: The Servant of God was filled with charity toward her neighbor, whom she loved for God. The works instituted by her are eminently works of charity, such as free assistance to the sick and the asylum for poor orphan girls in danger. Personally she went to the sick, to whom she gave her assistance; many times of the sick girls, in need of care, she took them on her lap, dressed their wounds, cleaned them and kept them sheltered in the orphanage.

From a Sister of mine, the late Sr. Anna Eufemia, it was once reported to me that the Servant of God, in dressing the sores of a sick person, licked them with her tongue. The Servant of God had the salvation of souls greatly at heart and used to exhort us Sisters to busy ourselves in drawing the sick to receive the Sacraments; and in this regard she told us: «You must show yourselves with the sick always solicitous and diligent, and if sometimes they grumble you must increase your attentions and assiduous assistance: remember to consider the house of the sick person as a Church and as the vestibule of Paradise». When the Servant of God was informed of some sinner, she prayed and had the Sisters pray for his conversion, and if he was sick she went personally to him in order to cooperate in his conversion. So I know she did with a Lady in the Barracks of St. Stephen at Piacenza, with a Priest who had gone astray and was sick unto death, and with some gentlemen of high condition. Personally she attended to the religious instruction of the Sisters and with exhortations and counsels formed their spirit.

§ 793
Always prudent, both as foundress and as superior.

Ad 25: Prudence shone admirably throughout the life of the Servant of God. For the time when she lived in the world and was a young girl, then a wife, then a mother, as far as I learned from persons of her family, and especially from her mother, she always gave proof of good sense, maturity of judgment and, above all, of exemplary life and edifying exactness in the fulfillment of all her duties. Having become then Foundress and Superior of our religious Community, she always let herself be admired for her irreproachable conduct, for her religious observance, for the way she governed those under her, who always held her as a provident mother. She was most watchful in the choice and admission of the Novices, in assigning the Sisters to the individual offices, and in providing for the good running of the Community and of the works entrusted to it. Also in preventing and correcting inconveniences and abuses she always gave proof of watchfulness, of discretion and of truly admirable judgment: and it is a fact that never, as far as I know, was a scandal deplored that could be charged to lack of prudence on her part. All this I depose from what I know and from what I learned in the Community. And from the whole of the information I have on the matter I formed the judgment that her prudence was not human, but proceeded from a much higher principle; nor ever, as far as I know, did she transgress the just limits of Christian prudence.

§ 794
Just toward God and toward men.
§ 795
She governed without partiality or favoritism.

Ad 26: In justice too the Servant of God was irreproachable. She observed with exemplary exactness her duties toward God, and lived in perfect conformity to the divine will. This was the constant norm of her life, and this she always taught us who were under her. As to her neighbor, as I myself frequently saw, far from harming the rights of anyone, she showed great generosity in paying workmen and vendors: to those who came to work and to render service in our houses she wished that, besides the generous pay, lunch, breakfast and supper be given, and she watched that they were well treated. Several times she rebuked me, if I tried to haggle or economize on something in this regard. If sometimes for the upkeep of the community or of her works it happened that she contracted some debt, she was always most punctual in paying it, as far as I know and as I always heard in the Community; and since it happened sometimes that at the time of maturity she was not in a position to pay at once, she called the creditor, explained the circumstance to him, offered him the interest corresponding to the sum of the debt, and asked for delay in the return of the capital. It is a fact that she never defrauded anyone in the least, nor, as far as I know, did anyone ever remain discontented with the treatment received from her. In the government of the Community she was always exact in giving to each what was just, without partiality or favoritism, as is known among us. She was moreover most careful not to say a word nor to permit others to say one to the detriment of anyone: and several times I myself saw, with edification, the readiness with which she deftly turned the conversation aside when she noticed that it might end in criticism or murmuring against the neighbor. She was always grateful to benefactors, always delicate in sentiments of friendship, always sweet, affable, attractive with everyone. It seemed, as we always said among ourselves, that the Lord had endowed her with a special gift of attractiveness, she exercising a charm by her insinuating gentleness.

§ 796
Temperate and mortified.

Ad 27: The Venerable was most temperate; she did not go in search of pleasant things, nor shrink from the unpleasant ones. Although she sat at the common table, she did not eat what was served to the Community, but was accustomed to take a soup seasoned with salt alone and sometimes with butter, cheese or oil and rarely with an egg, which we added with secret ingenuity and not at her wish; indeed I remember that, noticing it, she rebuked us. As a second dish she used a little vegetable. Besides continual abstinence from meat, she never ate fruit, nor drank wine or liqueur, she took no breakfast, sipping in the morning simply a cup of coffee without sugar; at supper she ate a little salad. Such a manner of diet she always kept, even when she was sick. Both I and my Sisters were convinced that she did all this for penance, whereas she said that she observed that manner of life because fatty foods made her ill.

§ 797
Mortifications and instruments of penance.

The Servant of God used instruments of penance; I, who had charge of the linen, noticed that the chemise of the Servant of God bore the imprint of a belt, with stains of rust, blood and pus, so that even after the washing, to remove the rust stains perfectly I used salicylic acid. The said stains were observed not only by me but also by the Sisters assigned to the laundry, among whom I recall Sr. Anna Virginia Gaggi and Sr. Anna Orsola, who at present I do not know in which house of our Institute they dwell.

She slept very little and spent a great part of the night in prayer, as I myself observed several times, as I deposed before. Her bed was made of a straw mattress, unlike the other Sisters who also had a wool mattress, which straw mattress was laid on two boards that rested on bare ground. A few rough chairs and an old wardrobe formed then all the furnishing of the room of the Servant of God, who used to keep her room always closed, permitting access to no one, and which I visited once on a chance occasion, having had to put back in place her straw mattress, remade at the insistence of us Sisters.

§ 798
She did not yield to human respect in the exercise of the virtues.

Ad 28: The Servant of God was endowed with Christian fortitude. When it was a matter of the glory of God and the exercise of the virtues she never yielded to human respect. With firmness and gentleness she required the observance of the Rules and of internal discipline. In tribulations and in her long illnesses she was always resigned, always keeping the evenness of her spirit.

§ 799
Model of modesty and chastity.

Ad 29: The Servant of God was our model in the virtue of purity and modesty, in speaking, in dealing, in acting, and with severity she required its observance in all those under her. In dealing with outside persons she had such an attitude of modesty as to seem Our Lady of Sorrows. It is a fact, moreover, that her life was a continual mortification, as I deposed before.

§ 800
Evangelical poverty.

Ad 30: The Servant of God was a lover of poverty, had no attachment of any kind, shunned every particularity in her capacity as Superior, and used for things of use the wardrobe in common like the other Sisters; indeed many times, not bearing it well that the Servant of God wore habits too worn, I had them prepared without her knowledge, using for the proper measurements my own person, I being almost of her build. She instilled moreover in all of us the spirit of poverty, though she was solicitous in providing us with everything, letting our Community lack nothing.

§ 801
Most obedient to ecclesiastical superiors.

Ad 31: The Servant of God, as her mother, Signora Adelaide, reported to me, was always docile and obedient; indeed the said Signora called the Servant of God, her daughter, a pearl. She was most obedient to ecclesiastical Superiors, whose dispositions she always carried out. When some disposition of the local Bishop did not seem just to us Sisters, the Servant of God wished that it be obeyed without discussion, and said that Superiors must always be obeyed, for if they err they are the ones responsible. She held in great veneration the person of the Roman Pontiff, and I, who accompanied her sometimes, saw with what devotion and respect she presented herself at the audience of the Holy Father, a respect she instilled in all of us, and docility and respect toward everyone was a characteristic note of the Servant of God.

§ 802
She performed the lowliest services in the community.

Ad 32, Proc. fol. 211: From the whole tenor of her life I can depose that the Servant of God held herself as the servant and the last of all, so humble was she. She lowered herself, though Superior, to the lowliest services of the Community; and I saw her sweep the floor, prepare food in the kitchen, make bread and other things. She thought so lowly of herself that one day she said: «After my death throw this body of mine away like a rotten dog», an expression that made too great an impression on us Sisters and moved us to tears.

§ 803
She practiced the virtues in an extraordinary manner.

Ad 33: The Servant of God, as I know, as I have already deposed, practiced all the Christian virtues not in a common and ordinary way, but in an extraordinary and superlative way, so as to surpass the common run of pious and virtuous souls, which means in a heroic degree, as you instructed me and I understand, and this until her death. In fact in the community she was always an example of observance and of virtue and for us Sisters it sufficed simply to see her to be seized with the greatest veneration for her.

Ad 34: I have never seen, known or read that the Servant of God, in the exercise of the Christian virtues, ever fell into any excess or exaggeration or made herself, through penances and mortifications, little suited to the discharge of her duties.

Ad 35: The Servant of God was enriched by God with extraordinary gifts.

§ 804
Held as a religious of uncommon virtue.

Ad 43, Proc. fol. 229v.: The Servant of God was esteemed in the Community as an uncommon religious for her singular virtues and gifts, so that for us Sisters any word of the Servant of God was a law, such was the respect professed toward her. When I was near the Servant of God at Piacenza I was able to observe that the Servant of God enjoyed the same esteem and opinion among the leading Ladies of Piacenza, so much so that the Marchioness Caracciolo of Piacenza, as I recall, enchanted by the virtues of the Servant of God, bequeathed a very rich patrimony to the Institute founded by the Servant of God. Such reputation and opinion was confirmed after the death of the Servant of God and I remember that the Marquis Pietro Caracciolo, who came to Rome expressly because of the grave condition of the Servant of God, took part in the funeral. Such reputation for holiness holds in all the houses of the Institute and among all who had occasion to deal with her. I have never known that anything was done to arouse or increase such reputation for holiness enjoyed by the Servant of God, which up to now has always remained constant and unaltered. I, for my part, have always held the Servant of God as a Saint and as such I hold her, so much so that I profess a particular devotion to her as to a mother.

§ 805
Grace attributed to the Servant of God.

Ad 45: From some Sisters coming from Rome and passing through Naples, whose names I am unable to specify or remember, when the present Process of beatification was about to open, speaking naturally in praise of the Servant of God, the following fact was told to me: In the Generalate House in Rome a Postulant of ours, whose name I think I was not told, had trouble with a finger, so that she was obliged to be treated at the clinic, where she went two or three times a week. But every treatment proved vain, and the trouble progressed so that the arm became swollen and blackish up to the elbow, and the doctors decided that the finger must be amputated so as not to run the risk of greater harm, and without the patient's knowledge it was decided for the next day. The matter, after several hesitations, was revealed by the local Superior to the sick Postulant, who was so distressed that she burst into tears, also because she feared that they would not afterward keep her in the Institute. That evening, the pain having increased and become intolerable, the Superior, to comfort her, gave her a little picture of the Servant of God to apply with faith, and so it was done. During the night the said sick girl saw in a dream a Sister of majestic appearance come forward who took an interest in her sufferings and told her to be at peace because she would be healed without recourse to amputation and that she would be a daughter of St. Anne, and so saying with her hand she marked her on the forehead with the sign of the cross, and the sick girl, who until then had suffered grave spasms, felt relieved, no longer feeling pain, and the next day with great joy announced to her Mistress that she was healed. At first she was not believed, but then, the nurse arriving for the dressing, the arm was found deflated and the hand as in a normal state except for a small scar. Taken to the clinic as agreed, the doctors ascertained that there was no longer need of an operation, she being healed, and ordered her to use only hygiene and cleanliness on the hand.

§ 809
She chose suitable persons for the offices.

Ad 17: As far as I know, I depose that the Servant of God sought with rectitude to assign to the various offices of the community the most suitable persons.
