§ 810
Despite her frail health she visited the communities.

Ad 18: I know from my own knowledge that the Servant of God, many times a year, undertook journeys to visit our various Houses in Italy; therefore I remember having learned of her going to Calabria, to Sicily, to Naples and elsewhere. Notwithstanding the frail condition of her health, she did not abstain from the obligation of the visit and so she traveled and, even though suffering, never let it be glimpsed that she was tired. I know that the Servant of God, in agreement with Monsignor Scalabrini, the late Bishop of Piacenza, established at first a kind of orphanage for deaf-mute girls, to which afterward she wished to give a special religious habit for those who consented, and with the purpose that these new Sisters, unfit for other works, should attend to the adoration of Our Lord in the Sacrament. I visited this Institute at Piacenza, which as in the beginning so at present is directed and assisted by our Sisters. The Servant of God founded also at Piacenza an orphanage for poor girls.

§ 811
Reputation for holiness: visits to the tomb.

Ad 42, Proc. fol. 344v.: I have visited the Tomb of the Servant of God several times out of my own devotion, and I know that our Sisters who are in or go to Rome go to visit the Tomb of the Servant of God. I do not know whether the said tomb is visited by other people; I say, however, that the Servant of God remained in Rome few years, whereas at Piacenza, where she founded our Institute, she was very well known and esteemed. Finally, I know from having generally heard it in our Institute that from the time of the death of the Servant of God our Sisters have been accustomed to visit the Tomb of the Servant of God, always out of spontaneous feeling of devotion toward her.

Ad 43: I have heard it said by various persons, even lay people, whom I could not specify, that the Servant of God was an extraordinary woman both for her works of great charity and also for her virtues, so that whoever approached her took away the finest impression. In the Community, moreover, I have always heard the Servant of God spoken of with praise for her religious observance and also, according to common opinion, for the extraordinary gifts with which she was believed to be endowed by God. This opinion has become more firmly established after her death, so that in our Institute the Servant of God is generally held to be a Saint. I do not deny, however, as usually happens, that some among our Sisters, perhaps for not having been satisfied, judged the Servant of God ill, but this is a very rare case and one I could not even determine at the moment, since the general opinion is that which I have stated above, and it commonly holds in all our Houses wherever they are found. In this esteem of holiness the Servant of God was held by Cardinal Belmonte, present Protector of our Institute, by Canon Amirante of Naples, by Canon Covino of Teggiano, by Princess Fitalia of Palermo, and from all of these I heard the Servant of God spoken of with the highest praise as a Saint, besides so many others whom I could not specify at the moment. I, for my part, have always had and have veneration and esteem for the Servant of God as a holy religious.

§ 819
Supernatural gifts. Grace attributed to the Servant of God.

Ad opportunas interrogationes respondit: Being in our House at Piacenza as a Postulant I kept in my heart, without having revealed it to others, the desire to possess the images of the Heart of Jesus and of Mary. One day when I was thinking of it least, entering, I do not know for what reason, the room of the Servant of God, I found her intent on cutting sheets on which images of the Saints are reproduced. At first seeing me, the Servant of God, without my having spoken to her, chose from among the little pictures she had on her table the images of the Heart of Jesus and of Mary and, handing them to me, said: these are for you. I was not a little surprised and amazed at how the Servant of God could have known my secret desire and I could not restrain myself from expressing to her my very surprise and amazement. But at present I do not remember what the Servant of God had answered me. I, however, was convinced, and still am, that the Servant of God read my heart, as in other circumstances.

Another time I was in Naples, in our House then in via del Duomo, as Mistress of the novices, and after the cholera of 1884 the Servant of God came to Naples several times; having learned that in the House there was a Sister named Anna Fede, most gravely ill, so much so that she occupied the room of the gravely ill and was seized by such convulsions as to seem almost dead, and in this state she had lasted for several months, the Servant of God showed a wish to visit the sick woman and in fact went. Meanwhile, the other Sisters having been sent away for a little while, she remained for some time alone with the sick woman. Suddenly the said Sr. Anna Fede was seen coming out of the infirmary, agile and healthy, crying: I am healed, the mother, alluding to the Servant of God, has worked the miracle for me.

I met the same Sr. Anna Fede on the landing of the stairs of our House and uttered a cry of surprise on seeing her, since I knew her to be in grave condition, but the said Sister repeated that she had received a miracle from the Servant of God. In the Community it was said afterward that our attending physician, who was Doctor Della Corte, had affirmed that the healing of Sr. Anna Fede was a true miracle, and that he, as I was told, at the request of the ecclesiastical Superiors, issued a special certificate in the said terms.

Concept of holiness.

§ 825
General details of the witness and scope of her knowledge.

My name is Sr. Margherita, in the world Angiolina D'Arcangelo, daughter of Antonio and Maria Mattea De Vita, native of Casalnuovo, Province of Foggia, aged 57; I am a religious of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne and I hold the office of doorkeeper in the Provincial House of Naples at Villa Cosenza at Ponti Rossi, where I live the common life. I have already been Superior in various Houses.

p. 537

Ad 7: In the year 1880 I applied to become a sister in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne. I was accepted and, in company with my late father, I went to Piacenza to the central House where the first time I had the pleasure of seeing the Servant of God Sr. Rosa Gattorno, Foundress and Mother General of the said Institute. From the very first sight of her I had a most pleasing impression because of her venerable appearance. The same impression it made also on my father. I remained from then on in the House at Piacenza where I stayed about two years. Then I changed several houses and in more than one of them I acted as Superior. By reason of this office I was in continual relation with the Servant of God, both by letters and personally.

In dealing with her, my veneration for her grew ever greater. What therefore I shall say in this examination is what I know from my own knowledge and what I have been able to hear in our Community.

Ad 10 ad 14: I, as I have said, came to know the Servant of God after the foundation of our Institute and therefore I can say nothing about what you ask me in these interrogatories.

I only often saw in our Houses the Mother of the Servant of God, the children and other persons of the family. From my fellow religious, moreover, Marianna Angelica, who knew her personally, it was reported to me that the Servant of God, before the foundation, was a married woman, but I do not know the particulars, that she was directress of the Daughters of Mary in Genoa and that she discharged this office with zeal, charity and edification of all who knew her. In this office she gave conferences to the Daughters of Mary, always with great humility and doctrine.

In coeteris I have nothing to add to what has been deposed.

§ 826
Foundation, purpose and title of the Institute.

Ad 15: I know that the Servant of God founded our Institute in the city of Piacenza and it was reported to me in the Community that she determined on this foundation because St. Anne had appeared to her, as is still seen from a painting kept in the House at Naples where I have lived for about four years, and there I found it.

Ad 16: Our Institute has as its purpose, besides one's own sanctification, to educate girls by means of religious and literary instruction, to assist the sick, men and women, both in public Hospitals and in private Houses, where we are called. Moreover we have the assistance and direction of prisons and of asylums for women. As I have learned, the Servant of God wanted to give our Institute the title of the Immaculate, but then in fact she placed it under the invocation of St. Anne and, as was reported to me in the Community, it was the Supreme Pontiff Pius IX who, in a visit made to him by the Servant of God, exclaimed on seeing her: «Here is a Daughter of St. Anne», and so the title remained to the Institute.

I was also told that the Pope added: «Your daughters will spread widely». While the Servant of God was still living, our Institute had great increase and spread rapidly in many cities of Italy and also in the Americas.

After her death it spread also in France, in Spain and in Africa, where, as far as I know, a house was opened even during the life of the Servant of God. The Servant of God herself, as I learned in the Community, wrote the Rules for our Institute, which were approved also by the Holy See, while she was still living. In our Institute the three vows of religious profession are made, temporary or perpetual according to circumstances. I know that the Servant of God also made these vows.

§ 827
Prudent and charitable superior.

Ad 17: I know it because it is notorious in the Community that the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno was the Foundress and first Superior General of our Institute, an office which she had to accept out of obedience to the Holy Father Pope Pius IX. In the discharge of this office I remember that she was always full of charity and prudence, alien to every spirit of superiority or domination and wholly intent on procuring the glory of God and the good of the Community. Her speech was always of a submissive, humble form and of holy unction, having always Jesus Crucified on her lips. Even when she had to correct she used the most benevolent forms and if at times she seemed a little austere, she did so to maintain the prestige of the Community, out of zeal and to train us in the observance of the Rules. I, who was received by her into the Community, remember the cautions she took to admit me and the benevolent words addressed to my father and also to me on that occasion. The same she practiced with the others who asked to be admitted to our Institute. Her particular concern was that nothing be lacking for the upkeep of us religious, and she treated us as a true mother. No different prudence and discretion she used in the choice of persons for the various offices of the Community and she saw to it that particular relations and friendships be avoided, especially with persons outside the Institute. The Servant of God had particular care of the sick Religious, and I, having been ill at Ferrara, remember that she sent a special religious to assist and care for me, and, writing to me or speaking to me when I was Superior, she inculcated charity toward the Sisters and several times told me not to mind economy in caring for the Religious and keeping them content.

§ 828
She bore every discomfort in the government of the Institute.

Ad 18: As long as the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno was in health, she often traveled to visit the various Houses of our Institute and to pro-

vide for its improvement, bearing every inconvenience and discomfort. I remember that she visited the Houses of Naples, of Ferrara, of Florence, of Sicily and particularly that of Rome; not excluding the House of Genoa, where she was born.

Besides what has been said, I remember that Monsignor Scalabrini, Bishop of Piacenza, entrusted to the Servant of God and through her to our Institute the work of the Deaf-mutes; as it is also known to me that to the confidence of the Servant of God other works were entrusted by Municipalities or by private persons, that is, Infant asylums, Orphanages, Municipal Schools, Hospitals, Asylums for the insane and Prisons.

All these works she accepted with all charity and great satisfaction of her soul, to give increase to the Institute and glory to God. All these works, in the life of the Servant of God, flourished beautifully and, except for one that has ended, even after her death have remained flourishing; indeed they have progressed and progress daily.

Ad 19: I am intimately convinced that the Servant of God, throughout the whole time of her life, always observed the precepts of God and of the Church and the obligations of her own state, always zealous for the glory of God and the good of souls.

Ad 20: I am sure that the Servant of God, from what I have seen and heard, was a virtuous woman and practiced the virtues until death.

§ 829
Heroic faith and apostolic spirit.

Ad 21: The Servant of God was filled with theological faith, and this virtue appeared in her speaking and in her acting. In all circumstances she said words that revealed her union with God and the fervor of her spirit. She had particular concern that religious sentiment be preserved among the peoples, and this was the principal purpose of the foundation of her Institute. She inculcated in all of us her Religious the sentiment of edifying our neighbor by our good example and of cooperating that sinners might return to God.

It was reported to me in the Community that when she opened the Mother House at Piacenza she wished, among other works, to gather the children of the people to instruct them in religious matters and educate them in the Christian way, and she was all joyful when she heard that good was being done by her Daughters. Whenever she spoke with us she always spoke spiritual and edifying words which revealed her piety and devotion. She had great care for the decorum of the House of God and I remember that when I entered the Community, in the House at Piacenza there was a simple internal Oratory; but by the commitment and zeal of the Servant of God a church beautifully adorned was built also inside the House, which inspires devotion in whoever enters it, and when the House in Rome was built it was her first thought to build an external Church, furnishing it with all that is necessary for the worship of God. I saw her several times in the Church, before the Most Blessed Sacrament, recollected in a particular manner, and especially at the moment of Communion she was seen in such an attitude as to arouse edification in all of us, and she remained for a long time so recollected as to seem almost in ecstasy, so that no one dared approach her, for any reason, at those moments.

I remember that, a year after I had entered the Institute, my parents came to see me and while we were together with the Servant of God conversing in the parlor the signal was given that Benediction was being given in the Church. Then the Servant of God, without more ado, rose from her place and ran without delay to the Chapel, leaving my parents in great edification at the fervor she showed in going to receive the blessing of Jesus Christ. She also inculcated veneration of the Most Blessed Sacrament: in this regard I remember that Sr. Anna Sofia told me that, being in the service of our Chapel, she used to leave without adoring Jesus. Once the Servant of God was there and called the said Sister and made her observe the obligation to stop to adore the Most Blessed Sacrament at least with the recitation of three Glorias.

The Servant of God was full of respect and veneration for the Pope, for the Bishops and for all ecclesiastical Authorities.

She had particular devotion to the Most Blessed Virgin and saw to it that a Chapel be dedicated to the Immaculate of Lourdes in the Church of our House at Rome. She had then a quite special devotion to our mother St. Anne and established that the month of July be celebrated in her honor in all our Houses, like that which the faithful make for Our Lady in May.

§ 830
Hope: she did not act from human aims.

Ad 22: Christian Hope was great in the Servant of God. From the way she spoke and from the irreproachable and active life she led, it was clearly seen that she had no earthly aims, but aspired solely to the attainment of eternal goods. She had contempt for worldly things and it is a fact that she went modestly dressed. I have heard it said in the Community that difficulties were not lacking to the Servant of God in the foundation and in the life of our Institute; but she went forward trusting only in God, nor ever failed in this trust as far as I know. She always inculcated in us this virtue of hope and trust in God: and this she did also with me when I laid before her some difficulty of the House of which I was Superior.

§ 831
Far from sin, conformed to the divine will.

Ad 23: From the whole of the words and actions of the Servant of God I deduce, with full conviction, that she was full of heavenly Charity. Not only have I never known that she fell into any fault, even slight and deliberate, but I know that the Servant of God felt great horror of sin. This is seen from the zeal with which she provided to avoid disorders in our Houses and to prevent also particular friendships among the Congregants, always recommending the faithful observance of the Rules and walking always in the presence of God: and she was always the first to give the example. Clearly appeared in her the perfect conformity to the will of God in all circumstances. The Servant of God was a woman of prayer and, not being able to occupy herself during the day praying much in order to fulfill her duties as Superior, she spent long hours of the night intent on fervent prayer, as far as I know and as my fellow religious have always told me. In our Community a common prayer book is used made expressly for us Daughters of St. Anne, which I believe was adopted by the will and initiative of the Servant of God.

§ 832
She loved her neighbor in God and sought to serve him.

Ad 24: The Servant of God loved her neighbor in God, to whose spiritual and material good she chiefly devoted herself in the Foundation of our Institute, which proposes only works of charity. She treated us other Sisters with great charity, as I myself experienced, and ordinarily in doubtful and difficult matters we Sisters turned to the Servant of God because of the great confidence placed in her by all of us. I know finally that the Servant of God had Masses celebrated for our deceased Sisters and exhorted us to pray for them. She was full of charity especially toward the poor sick whom she cared for and exhorted us to care for free of charge, accepting at home only a cup of coffee and some alms freely offered: and for this purpose she sent us Sisters for assistance in the Hospitals and in private houses, a work that the Servant of God already did personally before and at the beginning of the foundation, as I have generally heard.

§ 833
Prudence in the direction of the Institute and the attached works.

Ad 25: The Servant of God was also adorned with Christian prudence, which she showed in the direction of our Institute and of the attached works and in dealing with the Sisters, especially when she saw herself obliged to give some reminder or reproof, which she did with such grace and manner as to be for us an example of Christian prudence, as I myself experienced.

Ad 26: As for justice toward others, I have never known that the Servant of God failed to give others what was due. Toward us Sisters she always showed herself grateful for the work we performed, and such gratitude she always had toward the persons who were benefactors of our Institute.

§ 834
Poverty, mortification and instruments of penance.

Ad 27: The Servant of God personally attended to the order and cleanliness of her room, as I observed personally. Her room was poorly furnished, with a low ceiling, and once, peeping through the keyhole of the door, I saw the Servant of God washing her hands in a basin that the least of the Sisters would not have used.

It was said in the Community that the Servant of God slept on a straw mattress filled with dry leaves and covered with two black shawls, without using sheets. She dressed without distinction and in the Community it was said that she had only a single habit. She ate little and always meatless, preferably ordinary foods.

From the same Sisters I learned that the Servant of God had in her room a large Cross, on which she lay down to pray and to recite especially the rosary.

I was also told that she used instruments of penance, and once a Sister assigned to collect the linen showed me a shirt of the Servant of God pierced with little holes at the loins and gave me to understand that it was a sign that the Servant of God used hair-shirts. When then the Servant of God died, the Sister infirmarian who assisted her tore off her the hair-shirts which through long use had become embedded in her body, as I have heard in general. I add, finally, that in our House at Piacenza, at the Servant of God's place in the refectory, wine was never prepared but only water, and our present Superior General Sr. Anna Celsa told me that the Servant of God liked salami very much, and that she prepared it for the others and that sometimes she smelled it to mortify herself, but without eating it.

Sr. Anna Marziale, our old Sister, told me that the Servant of God every Friday stayed withdrawn in her room, and many times the Sisters, knowing her to be suffering, insisted from the door of her room that she take some refreshment, and the Servant of God consented to take a cup of coffee without sugar. Furthermore, I remember that the room of the Servant of God communicated by means of a narrow wooden stair with the organ of our Church, where the Servant of God went, as I believe, to pray before the Most Blessed Sacrament.

§ 835
Fortitude in the foundation and in difficulties.

Ad 28: The Servant of God was adorned with Christian fortitude, as is seen from the work undertaken and brought to completion of the foundation

of our Institute. Moreover, suffering as she was in health, concealing her sufferings, she never failed to fulfill the duties inherent in her office, and I remember that, dealing sometimes with her about matters of the Community, I noticed that she was suffering and, having questioned the other Sisters, I learned that the Servant of God was ill with a tumor and that she never wished to be examined by doctors, and with great patience and resignation she bore her illness until death, never having left, up to the last, the direction of our Institute.

§ 836
Integrity and prudence.

Ad 29: So spotless was the conduct and bearing of the Servant of God that for us Sisters, in dealing with her, every idea escaped us that she could have been married. She had great modesty in her glances, and her conversations were always inspired by holy things, and for us Sisters she was a model and an example in this virtue.

Ad 30: I have already deposed that the Servant of God at Piacenza kept for herself a wretched little room where there was not even an ordinary window, but only a small little window; and also in Rome, in our Generalate House, the Servant of God had a modest room without pretensions.

She dressed neatly but without refinement and like the other Sisters; indeed it was said that the Servant of God had only one habit for herself. In the talks she gave us she always sought to instill these sentiments of Christian poverty.

Ad 31, Proc. fol. 414: The Servant of God was always obedient and respectful toward Priests and Ecclesiastical Superiors, and in this she was for us an example and a teaching.

§ 837
Evangelical humility.

Ad 32: The Servant of God was very humble. She had with us Sisters ingratiating manners and a gentle and quiet speech, and I never saw her angry; in dealing with her one never noticed the slightest hint of a feeling of pride: and for us Sisters she was always an example in this virtue, exhorting us to practice it, saying that by the exercise of this virtue one succeeds in doing much good.

§ 838
Extraordinary gifts.

Ad 33: From the whole of the life of the Servant of God and from the zeal she had in bringing to completion our institution solely to glorify God and do good to her neighbors, I hold the Servant of God to be an extraordinary woman in the exercise of virtue, in which she persevered until death, so as to make herself singular among the other Sisters, even pious and good ones: which, in my belief, means heroism of virtue, as you instruct me and I understand. For the rest, if I am mistaken in this judgment of mine, it is notorious that in our Community the Servant of God was held to be a Saint.

p. 545

Ad 35: From Sr. Anna Marziale it was reported to me that one day the Servant of God invited the late Fr. Tornatore to follow her on a journey to one of our Houses. It was a Feast day, a thing contrary to her habits because she never traveled on Feast days, but it was urgent because in that House, as she said, a daughter of hers was betraying her. And in fact the matter was found true and the Servant of God provided for it. She had been able to know that disorder only by supernatural means, for it was unknown to all.

Ad 37: I know, from having heard it in the Community, that the Servant of God gave to the press a book, concerning I do not know what, and that moreover it was withdrawn before the S. Congregation. The Servant of God wrote to me several times on account of my offices discharged in the Community; but I have never known that in these or other writings attributed to the Servant of God there is anything contrary to faith or sound morals.

§ 839
Holy death, burial and reputation for holiness.

Ad 38: The Servant of God died in our House in Rome on 6 May 1900, as I remember, following a nephritic colic that lasted six days. It was reported to me that the Servant of God showed herself most resigned and received the Holy Sacraments and that shortly before dying she rose from her bed and, before the Crucifix or the Madonna, I do not know which, made the offering of our Institute.

Ad 39: In the Community I learned that the Corpse of the Servant of God was exposed in the Church of our House in Rome, where the funeral was celebrated, in which our Sisters took part in great numbers, having come there from our various Houses.

Ad 40: The Corpse of the Servant of God, as is notorious in the Community, was interred in the Cemetery of Rome and was later transferred to a special sepulchral Chapel built at the expense of our Community.

Ad 41: I have never heard or known that in the exposition, burial or recognition of the corpse of the Servant of God, around her sepulchre or elsewhere, anything of public cult or undue veneration was said, done or written.

Ad 42: When I was in Rome I went spontaneously, out of affection for the Servant of God, to visit her tomb to pray. I know that the same tomb is visited by others but I know no particulars, as I am not in Rome.

Ad 43: The Servant of God in life enjoyed a reputation for holiness among our whole Community and outside it. This reputation for holiness was confirmed by her death and still endures spontaneous and unaltered.

In the Community it is said that the Servant of God was held in great esteem by the Holy Father Pius IX, of h.m. I, for my part, have always considered her and consider her a Servant of God.

In coeteris I have nothing to add to what has been deposed.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 418v., testis respondit:

My name is Carlo Amirante, son of Saverio and Rosalia Iamas, born in

p. 547

Soverato on 1 September 1852, I am Canon Parish Priest of S. Maria Maggiore in Naples, where I live and have my domicile on the proceeds of my Benefice and on other family property.

Ad 7: I came to know personally the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, Foundress of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, toward the end of the year 1884, on the occasion of the Servant of God's coming to Naples, to the House of her Institute in Via Duomo. I was presented to her by His Eminence Card. Belmonte, then a simple Monsignor. Afterwards I had various commissions toward the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne in this House of Naples.

I was Teacher of literature to the Sisters to prepare them for examinations, then I was first extraordinary Confessor and then ordinary of the Community, and then director of the same Community of Naples for several years; therefore I always had occasion to approach the Servant of God and I received from her many times some commission of preaching or other for her Institute, and thus I was on special Mission also in the House at Piacenza, with the proper faculties of the S. Congregation and of the local Bishop, Monsignor Scalabrini.

Ad 16: The character of the Institute founded by the Servant of God is absolutely charitable, proposing primarily the free assistance of the poor sick, also at home, for which the Sisters may not ask any remuneration whatever. This Institute began to take shape in the House at Piacenza under the auspices of the local Bishop, Monsignor Scalabrini. Later the Daughters of St. Anne were also given teaching and some other pious office, such as taking in and assisting orphans and accompanying corpses to their last dwelling.

The habit worn by the Sisters was devised by the Servant of God herself, who then gave her Institute the name of Daughters of St. Anne. The Servant of God personally wrote the Rules of the Institute, as I have always been assured in general by the Sisters and by Cardinal Verga himself: and I am sure that the Servant of God always sought and obtained the approval of the Ordinaries on the Rules, since she did not act without taking obedience and approval from Ecclesiastical Authority. These Rules were then long discussed by the Holy See, until on the 25th anniversary of the Clothing of the Servant of God Cardinal Verga, Protector of the Institute, presented them to her as a gift, the said Rules definitively approved by the Holy See. According to the same Rules the usual three simple and temporary vows are made and after ten years perpetual ones may be made. From all the Sisters contemporary with the Servant of God I learned that the Servant of God made the vows of the Institute and submitted herself to all its Rules, which she observed faithfully. In my belief the Servant of God must have made also some other vow concerning abstinence, because it is known to me not only by the common voice of the Daughters of St. Anne, but also because I took part in the dinner of the Servant of God by chance and sometimes unexpectedly, since she had a portion of her dinner served to me in my room, as the Sisters assured me, and I observed that the Servant of God abstained from the use of meat or of any meat extract, and this I do not believe she did out of mere devotion, because she never came to violate it.

The Institute of the Servant of God had great development and rapid increase, so that during the life of the Servant of God Houses were opened in very many cities of Italy and also abroad, as in Bolivia, in Peru and in Africa, and at the death of the Servant of God there were counted almost ten thousand Sisters, and still today the same Institute is in full vigor.

§ 842
Superior zealous to the point of sacrifice.

Ad 17: It is notorious that the Servant of God was the first Superior General of her Institute. I do not know how this came about, but it is known to me that the Servant of God did not even want to be called Foundress and often showed me the desire that someone else had taken on her office. It is known to me from my own knowledge that the Servant of God discharged her office with zeal to the point of sacrifice; even when ill, when it was a matter of providing for or dealing with things concerning her Institute, she was always ready and did not think of herself.

Toward the Sisters the Servant of God was absolutely, in every respect, like a mother and in the needs both spiritual and temporal of the Sisters I can depose with all knowledge and conscience that the Servant of God never failed in her duty.

As to the reception of postulants, she was most watchful and most prudent, she did not look at birth, but weighed with great diligence above all morality.

For the life of the Sisters the Servant of God provided with the Institute's own

p. 549

means, until the S. Congregation established a certain dowry to be offered by those who asked to become part of the same Institute, and I remember that the Servant of God was authorized by the same S. Congregation to limit herself to not less than five hundred lire. She took great care to put suitable Sisters in the offices, and if at times inconveniences occurred she was very prompt to provide, and in this she never had prejudices, but always acted with rectitude.

§ 843
Prudent strictness in government.

She showed herself most strict toward the Sisters that they might not have or foster particular friendships, and she was immensely displeased when she came to know that some Sister went to the parlor without the attending Sister, and so she did not fail to make timely and severe reproofs. She provided moreover that the Sisters be well placed, and when she could not personally, informed by means of reports, she provided in due time. She watched that the Sisters always dress with simplicity, but decently. She felt great sorrow for the sick Sisters and informed herself and gave orders that they lack nothing in spiritual and temporal assistance. To the Superiors of the individual Houses she used always to say: «Have pity on the sick Sisters». She established various Infirmary Houses for the Sisters and I especially remember that of Piacenza, Gargatano, Naples and Palermo.

§ 844
She undertook frequent journeys to visit the communities.

Ad 18: The Servant of God, as is known to me from my own knowledge, undertook frequent journeys to visit the various Houses of the Institute. And this she did even in poor conditions of health, and I know that during the journey she suffered greatly because she was seized by severe migraine, but nevertheless the Servant of God did not complain of it. By the will of the Secretary and of the Assistant Sisters the Servant of God traveled in 1st or 2nd class, but I am convinced that the Servant of God, had she been able, would gladly have traveled in 3rd class, since many times she made remonstrances to the contrary, saying that it was against poverty, but ended by obeying her Sisters. I know that she often visited the principal Houses, and when she could not go to the secondary Houses, she had the local Sisters come to the neighboring principal Houses and listened to them and then provided as the case required. Such journeys she undertook until the last years of her life, and it is known to me from my own knowledge, having been present sometimes, that during the journey the Servant of God kept very recollected in a corner and exercised herself in prayers and crocheted little shawls for the poor.

p. 550

I know that in Piacenza there is a House of Deaf-mute girls kept and assisted by the Daughters of St. Anne, but I know no particulars, either of the foundation or of its organization.

§ 845
Reputation for holiness in life.

Ad 19: I always heard the Servant of God spoken of with praise before she was a religious, and her own brothers, little practicing in matters of piety and religion, told me that they had a holy sister. For the time that I knew and approached the Servant of God I can depose with full conscience that she exactly observed the precepts of God and of the Church and the obligations of her own state, always zealous for the glory of God and the spiritual good of souls.

Ad 20: The Servant of God was eminently virtuous and practiced all the Christian virtues until her death.

§ 846
Uncommon faith even before being a religious.

Ad 21: The Servant of God, by her speeches, in her Works, in her bearing, showed herself animated by an uncommon theological faith. I know, from having heard it, that the Servant of God, from her secular days, exercised in the Hospital of Genoa the apostolate of teaching catechism to the sick. This apostolate she continued, both for herself and for those dependent on her, when she became a religious, and I remember that in the Church of the Generalate House in Rome catechism was taught on feast days, and the Servant of God took part.

§ 847
Devotions born of the spirit of lively faith.

The Servant of God had great devotion to the Most Holy Trinity and wrote a prayer to the Eternal Father which was later adopted in the Institute. She had a most special devotion to the Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ and always repeated the phrase: «in my dear Crucifix», as she also concluded her letters with this expression: «I greet you and bless you in my dear Crucifix», according to the persons to whom she wrote. The Servant of God loved greatly the decorum of the House of God and I am a witness of it, especially for the two Houses in immediate dependence on the Servant of God, that is, the House of Rome and that of Piacenza, and it can be inferred from the way in which she took care to furnish the respective churches.

She had great devotion to the Most Blessed Sacrament and I, who had occasion to be in the two aforesaid Houses, was able to observe that the Servant of God several times a day went to visit Jesus in the Sacrament in the Church and there was no case of her going to table without having visited Jesus in the Sacrament. From the other Sisters in general it

p. 551

was reported to me that the Servant of God went to visit Jesus Christ even at night. She attended the Divine Sacrifice with great recollection and always kneeling although her condition of health did not permit it. She approached Holy Communion with such an attitude as to show extraordinary dispositions and recollection, as I was able to observe having sometimes administered Holy Communion personally to the Servant of God, and I received a great impression from it. As also she always put first a fitting preparation and afterward remained a long time giving thanks to Jesus Christ, always keeping the same attitude, which she also preserved on leaving the Church after her Communion.

§ 848
Heroic hope.

Ad 22: The Servant of God was adorned with Christian hope, which she showed by timely exclamations: «All is vain down here, — she said, — God alone is for us».

She lived detached from the things of earth and sacrificed even the love of her children: and guided by the desire for a perfect life she decided on the foundation and put on the monastic veil herself too. And in this she never availed herself of human helps, but placed all her trust in God. And God alone, she said, must protect my Institute. In fact the anxieties she met, even financially, were not few, but the Servant of God never lost courage, owing to her full confidence in God.

§ 849
Conformed to the divine will: union with God.

Ad 23, Proc. fol. 426v.: On all the occasions on which I dealt with the Servant of God, I never perceived in her anything reprehensible. It is known to me, moreover, from personal experience, that the Servant of God always and unalterably preserved conformity to the divine wills, whether things favorable or sad were reported to her by me, given my office, or concerning the Institute, or the persons of her family. Her habitual word was: «Let us bless the will of God in his dear Crucified Son».

From the way the Servant of God attended Holy Mass, having myself offered the Sacrifice in her presence, it seemed to me, before and after, and more in the act in which she took part in the Holy Eucharist, that she was so recollected in herself as to leave me in doubt whether she was rapt in her senses, so great was the composure of her person, the attitude of her face, her fixed gaze. From this I infer that her mind fed on the divine truths.

As for vocal prayers, I was several times near her both in the private Chapel and in the public Church in Rome, and I observed that, besides always remaining kneeling and still, she pronounced the words with such affection that, ashamed of myself, I desired to know how to recite the Holy Office with the same attention, recollection, fervor of spirit and heartfelt piety.

With me, although with a smiling face, she let me understand that suffering is absolutely necessary, if one wishes to please God by conforming to his Will, in which true sanctification consists, and not to seek enjoyments: and the phrase she used to me one day, in gentle rebuke of my ignorance and weakness, has remained impressed on me: «Professor, you seek sweets, but to be saints one must dance on the cross!».

I saw her weep when I was obliged to report to her something of the conduct of sacred ministers or of her Sisters.

§ 850
Manifestations of charity toward neighbor.

Ad 24: As to Charity toward neighbor, both for the spirit and for the body, the Servant of God reached true and proper sacrifice. I am truly a witness of how she committed herself, when things came to her knowledge, to eliminate even possible scandals: and out of undeserved confidence in me, when she supposed that some Sister was troubled in conscience or in danger, she referred her to me and ipso facto, without regard for commitments, administrators or influential persons, removed her and moved her elsewhere. And sometimes she said to me: «Charity is ordered first to the interests of eternity, then to those of time. The greatest evil, indeed the only evil, is sin». She provided in fact and informed herself with care that spiritual aids not be lacking in the Houses: and it was for this that it fell to me to travel through a good part of Italy, always, however, with the consent of my Superiors.

Love for the poor, the suffering, the unfortunate was the counselor of the Work of the Servant of God. And this love, it is my deep conviction, she learned from the open wounds of her dear Crucified.

She did not tolerate comparisons between Institute and Institute; she was content with the little that could be done; as she said, the increase be-

p. 553

longs to God. She suffered oppositions, almost torments, because of the movements the Institute itself made in its branches: and having allowed myself sometimes to sympathize with her, I received this reply: «The poor suffer so much!»; and when I saw her at the bedside of dying Sisters, her soul was turned to God and she thanked him that another daughter was transplanted to heaven.

I know that she loved her slanderers and, as she was obliged to deal with me about some family questions and also concerning the Rules of the Institute, no word of resentment ever escaped her lips, and when things were most evident she said to me: «Professor, but let us pray for our opponents: do not forget that Jesus forgave from the cross his crucifiers».

§ 851
Held to be a most prudent woman.

Ad 25: I esteemed the Servant of God as a most prudent woman: first, because in the disagreements often occurring between her relatives and her work, she always smoothed them over in a tranquil manner, and especially with her two brothers; second, because in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, often exposed to malicious talk and to the oppositions of administrators, purveyors, etc., the Servant of God knew how to resolve matters in such a way that all remained satisfied. She was content at times with the closing of some House so as not to expose her Sisters to the possibility of calumnies and the like, as happened with the House in Nola and the House in the Ravaschieri Hospice in Naples; and also here in the Hospital of Peace. I know, moreover, that the Servant of God was slow to correct, because, not on first information, she always admonished with gentleness: when then she had made sure of the existence of the evil, she punished severely without showing herself severe, and this I was able to observe several times from my continual dealings with the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne. I am sure that the Servant of God showed herself adorned with this prudence until death.

§ 852
Exemplary spirit of justice.

Ad 26: As to Justice toward God, I refer to what has been deposed. As to Justice toward neighbor, I do not know that the Servant of God contracted debts, but it is known to me that she satisfied all. In my own person, moreover, it happened that, made perhaps in penance because I would not accept anything for the commitment I showed for her Community, she obliged her son-in-law, Count Barbiellini, to go to the station of Siena and pay for the first-class ticket confirmed to Rome, to make me rest, and continuing to Naples. Likewise, by means of the then Mgr. Belmonte, today Cardinal of the H. R. Church, she had a gold watch of 18 carats delivered to me, with a dedication to me engraved on the case, a watch which I keep with deep gratitude.

Finding myself often exposed to the censures of the malevolent, particularly in the Ravaschieri Paternal House, where I myself had granted the Sisters Daughters of St. Anne, she was content that the Sisters withdraw rather than that my dignity be diminished.

§ 853
Temperate and mortified.

Ad 27: As to Temperance, the Servant of God, as far as is known to me, never took sweets or other delicate foods; indeed in the presence of the Most Eminent Cardinals she never took anything that is said among us to be choice in the matter of food or drink, and with a certain manner and grace she avoided what was offered her. As I have said other times, I took part in her poor, frugal table, habitually meatless.

In clothing, which was always of the form of the Institute, she kept cleanliness, but poverty. The late Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega secretly provided her even with a handkerchief now and then. Into her room in Rome I entered on the occasion of her death and found it furnished with a few chairs, a wretched bed, a prie-dieu on which was a most beautiful Crucifix. At Piacenza I was always received in the study but the Sisters told me that the Mother's room was the receptacle of her sufferings, both of tears and of personal mortifications. I suppose that mortifications were not lacking to her, but she knew so well how to hide them that she never let them be perceived, at least by me, except once when she was seized by the so-called writers' cramp, and even so she concealed it with great diligence. I repeat that the late Fr. Agostino Donadio of the Minims said to me, jesting: my dear Professor, the Mother is not just any bigot, but is of manly virtue; and he said this alluding to her mortifications and virtues.

Ad 28: The Servant of God was adorned with Christian Fortitude.

§ 854
Courageous and strong in adversities.

It is notorious with what courage and firmness of soul she bore adversities, so that in the Holy Church of Jesus Christ her Institute might have

p. 555

done a little good. When, because of the openings and closings of Houses, she met oppositions, she took comfort in it as a demonstration of the will of God and, having recourse to the foot of her Crucifix, held firm to her decision. I remember that once, because I had obstinately opposed her counsel for the retention of a Superior, she resisted me strongly. And since I persisted she yielded out of prudence, but I had afterward to repent bitterly and, to my humiliation, had to return to her that she might set things right. Which she did.

§ 855
Modesty and integrity.

Ad 29: I saw the Servant of God always with eyes lowered or raised to heaven and with her arms always folded on her breast, when, rarely, she was not working; she never fixed her eyes on persons, so that the Sisters sometimes complained to me because the Mother did not look them in the face. I recall in particular that once, when I was with the Servant of God in the study room in the House at Rome, a Sister presented herself returning from the baths of Sampierdarena and with a certain hilarity uncovered one of her wrists, saying to me: «Look, Professor, how the sun has burned me!». And the Servant of God, with a severe air, reproved her, saying: «Ah! Ah! in the presence of a Priest; do not forget that you are a spouse of Jesus Christ!». This made a great impression on me and confirms me still more in the idea of the love she had for Chastity.

§ 856
She loved, practiced and greatly recommended poverty.

Ad 30: As to the virtue of poverty, which formed the object of her continual recommendations, I observed that the Servant of God kept great cleanliness in her clothing, but very often I saw her veil and her habit patched; using ordinary and cheap handkerchiefs; nothing refined in her study, except the image of the Crucifix, always beautiful; never accepting a gift, so that the immense offerings made to her on the twenty-fifth of her religious clothing were immediately distributed to the various Houses.

At this point I note that it was often said among some Sisters that those Superiors were dear to the Servant of God who gathered and economized most, even to the detriment of the Sisters, sending everything to the Generalate House to earn merit with the Mother. This, as far as I know, is perfectly false, and I prove it by the conduct of the Servant of God. At the opening of the House of the Morigerati, when Baron Pellegrini, of happy memory, and the late Mariano Belli handed over the small income assigned to the said House, the Servant of God did not even touch the securities, which were handed over to the late Sr. Anna Benedetta Carrega. When it was thought to buy a new House in via Capodichino, here in Naples, the Servant of God opposed it, giving as her reason the grave sacrifices to which the Sisters would be subject. I add that all the money that was paid to the Generalate House in Rome, as surplus from the other Houses, was destined for nothing else, as the aforesaid Sr. Anna Benedetta told me, than to meet the needs of other poor Houses and for the movement of the Sisters. There was also murmuring about this movement of the Sisters, as useless and, they often said, harmful. But I must in conscience affirm that these continual movements took place for the preservation of the Sisters' virtues, as the Servant of God confided to me several times, loving rather the reputation of the Institute than material well-being.

§ 857
Veneration and obedience toward authorities.

Ad 31, Proc. fol. 434: The Servant of God spoke with great veneration of the Holy Father and, toward the Cardinal Protectors of the Institute, was very submissive and respectful, so as to merit from them benevolence and a treatment beyond all words deferential, and among others I could cite the late Cardinals Alimonda, Verga and Sanfelice, men of the highest stature who certainly would not have taken the Servant of God into consideration if she had not offered reason of virtue and above all of obedience. The same respect, as far as I know, the Servant of God always showed to the local Bishops of the various Houses, to whose directives in every case she submitted.

§ 858
Enchanting humility.

Ad 32: The Servant of God thought lowly of herself and attributed to God everything concerning her work, and if at times she was given the title of Foundress: «Not at all, — the Servant of God would answer, — I am only an instrument in the hands of God: and who is it that does the work: the instrument or the hand that uses it?». This sentiment of humility the Servant of God sought to instill in those dependent on her, and, so that her Sisters might recognize themselves as nothing, she wished them to wear the cord of St. Francis of Paola, who called his Friars by the name of Minims.

p. 557

Witness XIX (II ex off.), Most Rev. Mgr. Carlo Amirante 557

§ 859
Equanimity at every moment.

Ad 33: I depose with great conviction of the equanimity always preserved by the Servant of God in adverse moments as in prosperous ones, whereby she let be glimpsed in the various contingencies an extraordinary patience and, in my belief, heroic, that is, beyond all praise and deserving of the deepest admiration.

For the rest, from the whole of her life I hold the Servant of God to be a religious of uncommon virtue.

Ad 34: I have never heard, known or read that the Servant of God in the exercise of the virtues ever fell into any excess or exaggeration; rather I can depose that the Servant of God discharged her duties with great diligence until her death.

§ 860
Holy death.

Ad 38: I remember that the Servant of God died in Rome on 6 May 1900 of a visceral illness. She received the last Sacraments, as was reported to me. Having had news in Naples of her grave state, of my own free will I went to Rome and found the Servant of God in very alarming condition, so much so that she did not respond to some word I addressed to her; I noticed, however, that she understood.

§ 861
Held in life to be a woman of uncommon virtue.

Ad 43: During the life of the Servant of God she was generally held to be a woman of uncommon virtue. There were also those who said that she was adorned with extraordinary gifts. Similar reputation she enjoyed also after her death, as she enjoys it still.

I know that many persons of every class and condition held the Servant of God in great esteem precisely for her virtues. Among these I name the late Cardinals Verga, Parocchi, Galimberti, Alimonda, Mgr. Francesco Vento and Mgr. Carlo Caputo, who were Bishops of Aversa, and Mgr. Zuccaro, who was Bishop of Caltanissetta, who I do not know whether is still among the living, and Doctor Albertazzi, attending physician of the House at Piacenza. Among the living let suffice for all His Eminence Card. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, who held and still holds her in the reputation of a true Servant of God.

This reputation was and is entirely spontaneous, based solely on the reports of the virtues of the Servant of God. It is known to me personally that this reputation prevails in Rome, Naples and Palermo.

For me the Servant of God was a virtuous woman, indeed most virtuous.

(EX PROCESSICULO ADDITIONALI DIANEN., ann. 1917)

SOLE WITNESS

Most Rev. Mgr. ANGELO RAFFAELE COVINO

Name, surname, date and place of birth: Angelo Raffaele Covino, born in 1851 at Teggiano (Salerno).

State and profession: Priest, Dean Canon of the Cathedral of Teggiano.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Age of the witness when he came to know the Servant of God: 36 years.

Age of the Servant of God when the witness came to know her: 56 years.

Ad 2 interr., Proc. fol. 389, testis respondit:

§ 862
General details of the witness and scope of his knowledge.

My name is Angelo Raffaele Covino, son of the late G. Battista and Maria Capobianca, native of Teggiano, aged 66, I am Dean Canon of this Cathedral of Teggiano, graduate in Sacred Theology and Domestic Prelate of His Holiness. Approved Confessor pro utroque sexu and also pro monialibus. Prosynodal Judge, examiner and co-visitor of the Diocese, former Episcopal Delegate of the late Bishop of this Diocese, Mgr. Tiberio. I live on my own means.

Ad 7: Around the year 1887 the Sisters called Daughters of St. Anne came here to Teggiano, called by the Charity Congregation of this town, to take care of the local Hospital. I was appointed by Monsignor Addessi, then our Bishop, as director and Confessor of the Daughters of St. Anne, and I obeyed.

p. 559

Sole witness, Most Rev. Mgr. Angelo Raffaele Covino 559

In this period of time the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno, Foundress and Mother General of the Sisters, appointed me also Protector of the same. For about two years we were in epistolary relation, always for the oversight and direction of her own daughters. Afterwards we saw each other personally in Naples only once, and she strongly recommended to me vigilance over her daughters here in Teggiano and that I make a conscientious report to her. From the first time I saw this Servant of God I had the impression of a holy woman, full of the charity of Jesus Christ and at the same time firm and strong in her government. I remained in conversation with her for a long time, and she urged me to direct only and exclusively her daughters of Teggiano and to leave another Community of which I also had the spiritual direction. We took leave (she saying to me: «My son» and I calling her: «Mamma»); as to the exhortation the Servant of God made me to leave the other Community, I am convinced that she was in this enlightened by God, because after a few months one of those Religious, for a just admonition I gave her, threatened to poison me, for which reason I, seized with fear, left the direction of those Sisters, and then I remembered the words the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno had said to me, which I took for a prophecy.

Afterwards, another single time, in Rome, I saw the said Servant of God. I was then in epistolary correspondence with her until a few years before her death. All that I shall say in this examination is what is known to me from my own knowledge and what I have heard also from other persons, and especially from her daughters.

§ 863
Veneration and recourse to the intercession of the Servant of God.

Ad 8: I nourish a very great and deep devotion toward this Servant of God, I continually have recourse to her intercession, and this since her death. I add that a few months after the death of the Servant of God, finding myself in Rome, a strong thought arose in my mind to do something in her honor. And so I bought flowers of enameled metal and chose those not funereal, and had a garland made of them to which I affixed an inscription on a plaque of the same metal, in which, in a few verses that I do not now remember, I summed up the whole life of Gattorno. This crown I had laid, and it is still seen on the tomb of the Servant of God at Campo Verano in Rome. I would rejoice greatly if the Church were to raise her to the honor of the Altars for the greater glory of God.

§ 864
Prudent, gentle and strong Superior.

Ad 17: It is a fact that the Servant of God was the first Superior General of her Institute and continued in this office until death. She exercised her office with much prudence, gentleness and fortitude.

The Sisters carry out their office in Hospitals and other Works, dependent on the Municipalities, on the Charity Congregations, and receive the corresponding emolument: and so their support is provided for, and this in general.

As to clothing, the Daughters of St. Anne always had a decent habit, which the Servant of God provided when they could not, because of the scantiness of the pay they received from the Municipalities or other contracting Bodies. The Servant of God took much care of her daughters in their temporal and spiritual needs, wishing that nothing be lacking to them; to this end, in the contracts she stipulated with the Municipalities, Charity Congregations or others, she had it inserted as a condition that those Bodies must provide the Sisters who fell ill with medicines and doctors and even, in case of death, the accompanying of their corpses and the burial. As for the spiritual part, she relied on the zeal of the Ordinaries of the places. All this is still practiced today.

§ 865
She accepted every kind of suffering for the good of the Institute.

Ad 18: It is known to me from my own knowledge that the Servant of God undertook various journeys to visit her religious, sparing neither discomforts nor privations nor sufferings, although she was of frail health. I know that she went several times, for the said visits, to Sicily and that in the region of Salerno she went for the same purpose as far as Eboli.

Ad 19: It is my conviction, from what I saw and heard of the Servant of God, that she, in every state of hers, observed the Precepts of God and of the Church and the duties of her own state. It is a fact moreover that I never heard anything to the contrary, she being always zealous for the glory of God and the good of souls.

Ad 20: I am convinced also, from what I have heard and learned from the many Daughters of St. Anne whom I have known, that the Servant of God practiced all the Cardinal, Theological and attached virtues.

Ad 21: I know from the cited sources that the Servant of God was animated by

p. 561

§ 866
Lively faith. Characteristic devotions.

lively faith. She was very zealous for catechetical instruction, and this is one of the branches to which her Religious devote themselves; she held in great esteem sacred things, religious functions, the decorum of the House of God and the furnishings and equipment of the Church.

Her particular devotion was to the Passion of Jesus Christ and to the Most Holy Crucifix. The Sisters told me that the Servant of God was most fervent in attending Holy Mass and especially in approaching Holy Communion. She took great care to provide for the administration of the Word of God to her Sisters, and begged the Bishops in whose Dioceses her Houses or her Works were located to send pious and zealous preachers to her Daughters.

The Servant of God always had great veneration for the Supreme Pontiff, for the Bishops and for Priests: this I learned both from conversations with her and from what the Sisters told me of it.

Most tender was the devotion of the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno to the Most Holy Virgin Mary, especially under the title of the Immaculate Conception: and it is known to me that she always recommended to her Religious to prepare for the feast of the Immaculate with a devout novena, and that this be made in their various Houses with as much solemnity as possible.

§ 867
Christian hope always animated her acting.

Ad 22: I have a high concept of the Christian hope that animated the Servant of God: she had aims

not earthly, without anxiety for temporal things: all her aspirations were for God and for eternal goods. In struggles, in anxieties or contradictions, all her trust was in God and in her Crucified, as she expressed it: and this she always instilled in her Religious, not to trust in human helps but to have recourse to Jesus in the Sacrament, to Jesus Crucified, and go forward with calm and tranquility.

§ 868
Full of divine love. Spirit of prayer.

Ad 23: As to charity toward God, I depose with full conviction that the Servant of God was full of divine love: her life was irreproachable and I never knew that she committed any voluntary fault.

She had her spirit always raised to God, always in union with God, always in perfect conformity to the will of God. All this I depose from what I myself saw and from what I always heard.

p. 562

She was devoted to prayer, and I was told that she was always the first in the Community in the exercises of prayer and in the practices of piety.

§ 869
Love toward the neediest neighbors.

Ad 24: The Servant of God was animated by charity toward neighbor, and this depended on the love she had for God, as is seen from the whole of her life and from the fact that she had partiality toward no one. The most beautiful and fullest proof of her charity toward neighbor is represented by the foundation of her Institute, which is all charity and sacrifice, directed to the bodily good of neighbor and through it to the spiritual good. A particular argument, then, of her holy love for her Religious I deduce, among other things, from this, that she herself wrote to me at times that the Sisters here should retain for their particular needs what was left over from the emolument they received from the local Bodies and which should have been paid into the general treasury: and I infer that she did so also with other houses of the Institute. As to suffrage for the souls in Purgatory, I depose that in the Rules of the Institute it is prescribed that each time the death of the Sisters be communicated to all the Sisters, inviting them to suffrage.

§ 870
Prudent, gentle and strong.

Ad 25: The Servant of God was endowed with Christian Prudence, which shone forth in the exercise of her office as Superior general.

I find that I have already deposed that she knew how to unite admirably gentleness with Fortitude. It is a fact moreover that I never heard the slightest complaint about her way of acting, even from some less exact religious.

I add that all the good that the Religious, her daughters, told me of her, far from constituting an exaggeration, as I believed before knowing the Servant of God, corresponded perfectly to her virtue; indeed it was little, in my judgment, as I was able to verify when I then came to know her.

Ad 26: As to the virtue of Justice toward God I refer to what has been deposed; as to that toward neighbor, I have never known that she in the slightest violated anyone's right. She showed herself most grateful toward me for the work I expended for her Daughters and I must believe that she did the same with other benefactors of the Institute.

The Servant of God was moreover most deferential to all authorities.

§ 871
Temperate and always balanced.

Ad 27: As to the virtue of Temperance, I must point out that the Servant of God was always equal to herself, both in prosperous things and in adverse, which shows the mastery she had over herself in moderating the movements of the soul.

She was most mortified in food, as also in rest, which was reported to me by the Sisters who were together with her. From the same Sisters I learned that at her death there were found near her instruments of penance and a kind of hair-shirt on the corpse, fastened to the breast on the side of the heart.

§ 872
She never failed in her duties out of human respect.

Ad 28: The virtue of Fortitude in the Servant of God results from the correction she made to those dependent on her, from never failing in her duties out of human respect, and from suffering the troubles and pains of her long-standing infirmities, always with resignation and without ever complaining of them, indeed without ever speaking of them and continuing to govern her Institute with energy; so that the news of her death came unexpectedly, although preceded by many and long sufferings which were virtuously concealed by her.

§ 873
Chastity and poverty.

Ad 29: As to the exercise of the Chastity of the Servant of God, I depose that she was most modest without affectation, and reserved in manner without roughness: when she spoke she did not fix her eyes on persons, but always had her eyes turned to heaven.

Ad 30: From what I have seen and heard I can assert that the Servant of God had the spirit of poverty. She was modest in dress from the time she was negotiating the foundation of her Institute with the Servant of God Pope Pius IX. He, precisely because of her poverty, used to give her the epithet «ragamuffin», which was reported to me by many Sisters.

Ad 31: As to the obedience of the Servant of God to Superiors, I have never known anything to the contrary.

Ad 32: As to humility, the Servant of God considered herself the last of all and I never heard her speak of herself and of the good she did. She used to inculcate in her Daughters this beautiful virtue of Humility, submission and their own nothingness.

§ 874
She practiced the virtues in an uncommon way.

Ad 33: The Servant of God, in my judgment, practiced all the Theological and moral Virtues, of which I have deposed, in an uncommon way and far superior even to pious souls, of whom I have known and know a great number: she exercised them in an extraordinary and superlative degree and always with constancy and ease: and this for me means in a heroic degree.

§ 875
Reputation for holiness in life and after death.

Ad 43: The Servant of God, in life and after death, has enjoyed and enjoys a reputation for holiness among all the Sisters of her Institute, and this reputation is entirely spontaneous, based solely on the report of her virtues and without any interruption, continuous. I do not know whether outside the Institute she has enjoyed or enjoys such a reputation. I, for my part, have considered and consider this Servant of God a true Saint.

Ad 45: I have often commended myself to the intercession of the Servant of God and have always experienced her protection. My confidence in her intercession grew some years after her death, precisely when Sr. Ermelinda Bianchi gave me a medal on which, on one side, an image of her is engraved and on the other of St. Anne, a medal which I have always carried and carry on me.

In particular I depose that twice in Naples I found myself in popular riots. Terror had invaded everyone, so that warehouses and palaces, at the approach of a furious crowd, were closed. I too was seized with great fear. The first time in Via Duomo, near the Church of the Sacramentine nuns, and the other time, in a carriage, in Piazza della Carità. The tumultuous crowd was pursued by the cavalry. And I rightly feared for my life. Then, gripping the medal of Gattorno, I invoked the Servant of God, saying: «Mamma Gattorno, do not let me die!». The fact was that both times I remained safe and sound, suffering merely strong jostling from all sides: the crowd passed as though without seeing me. I held and still hold that I remained safe through the intercession of the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno.
